stories.headline: 'Gukesh's lifetime dream just came too early': Levon Aronian assesses Sindarov clash
stories.deck: In an exclusive interview with TimesofIndia.com, American Grandmaster Levon Aronian assesses the upcoming World Championship clash between Gukesh and Javokhir Sindarov. He discusses the immense pressure on Gukesh after becoming the youngest world champion, Sindarov’s adventurous style, and the strategic battle ahead. Aronian also reflects on his own career, revealing why he has no regrets about…
stories.bodyText:
World Championship challenger Javokhir Sindarov is not thinking about the summit clash against Dommaraju Gukesh yet.
Earlier this year, the 20-year-old Uzbek earned his shot at the title by winning the Cyprus Candidates with a round to spare. But having returned to the country where it all began — it was in India that Sindarov won the FIDE World Cup in Goa in 2025 to qualify for the Candidates — he is keen to talk about everything except the upcoming Geneva encounter, where he will take on Gukesh in a series of 14 classical games running from November 22 to December 13.
"Right now, I'm focusing on my next events: the Global Chess League and the Olympiad," he told reporters on Friday. "After those, I will start preparing for the World Championship match."
The Global Chess League (GCL) begins on Saturday. The Uzbek Grandmaster plays for the American Gambits there, then turns out for his national team at the Olympiad in Samarkand from 15 to 27 September.
Gukesh will also represent India at the Chess Olympiad, but the GCL is one of several tournaments he has chosen to skip as he sharpens his focus on the World Championship match.
American Grandmaster Levon Aronian senses that the title fight between two 20-year-olds will hinge as much on temperament as on preparation.
"Gukesh is a big fighter," he told TimesofIndia.com during an exclusive interview. "He has been a bit down, but I expect him to be in a fighting mood for the match. Of course, it's a tremendous pressure."
Gukesh became world champion at 18, the youngest to do so. Aronian sees an echo of an earlier era in that. Mikhail Tal, who won the title at 23 in 1960, was himself the youngest world champion of his time, before Garry Kasparov broke the record 25 years later.
"You know, you're so young and your lifetime dream just came too early. I think the same kind of thing happened to Mikhail Tal. He also became a world champion too early. And of course, it's normal to be overwhelmed," Aronian added.
Mikhail Tal (Photo from Dutch National Archive)
From a strategic point of view, Aronian feels the wider chess world to have already made up its mind about how Gukesh will approach the match.
"I think people at the moment, they think that Gukesh is going to go and try to be very cautious, like in the similar style, like Ding (Liren) was doing against Nepomniachtchi, or also the way Ding was playing against Gukesh as well," he said with a smile.
Whether that script holds against Sindarov, he added, is the interesting question.
"There are so many choices to make, and it's definitely going to be an interesting match from a strategical point. I expect Sindarov to be continuing playing very interesting chess the way he's doing. It's an interesting clash, I think. Hopefully, there will be lots of resulting games," he opined.
Asked whether failing to win the World Championship title himself was a source of regret, Aronian, who has been ranked World No. 2 and has won world titles in every format except classical, concluded, "I have no regrets whatsoever, because I never valued myself so highly as a chess player. Of course, I have talent, and I'm better than many of the world champions in my understanding of chess. But the way I got to be number two is already a miracle for me; my knowledge of chess was so much worse before.
"I'm not sure that setting up goals is a good thing for you. Sometimes it just adds to the anxiety. I think it's better just to enjoy and cherish what you have."

stories.headline: Nepal floods: 5-year-old among three Indians rescued from Trishuli Bazaar area
stories.deck: MEA Spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal noted that 1,907 Indians have safely crossed over to Nepal from China
stories.bodyText:
Three more Indian nationals, among them a five-year-old child, have been rescued from the flood-hit Trishuli Bazaar area of Nepal, bringing the total count of Indian evacuees to 169, while 275 nationals remain missing, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said on Friday (September 4, 2026).
Sharing broader updates on the safety of Indian nationals, MEA Spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal noted that 1,907 Indians have safely crossed over to Nepal from China.
Also read | Nepal floods: Indian volunteers take relief to isolated communities
The three Indian nationals rescued from the Trishuli Bazaar area have been identified as Abhijit Suresh Pawar, Dipika Abhijit Pawar, and five-year-old Samarth Abhijit Pawar, Mr. Jaiswal said, adding that the Indian Embassy in Kathmandu is facilitating their return flight home.
The spokesperson said India has supplied around 95 tonnes of relief material to Nepal since the flash floods hit the country on August 26.
The death toll from the floods has risen to at least 1,295 after rescue workers recovered more bodies from affected areas, according to Nepalese authorities.
While emergency teams have rescued more than 12,000 people, roughly 5,000 remain missing as search and rescue operations continue.
"As per our information, 275 Indian nationals remain missing. We continue to be in close touch with the Nepali government," Mr. Jaiswal said at his regular media briefing.
"We deeply appreciate the efforts of the Nepalese authorities in this regard." Mr. Jaiswal said 169 Indian nationals have been rescued and 1,907 Indians have safely crossed into Nepal from China.
"As per official sources in China, there are no Indian travellers who are stranded in the Tibetan Autonomous Region in China," Mr. Jaiswal noted.
The MEA spokesperson said India will continue to provide assistance to Nepal as per the requirements of the government in that country.
"We do plan to send more forensic kits, Bailey bridges and other materials that are requested by the government of Nepal," he said.
Mr. Jaiswal said India has supplied around 95 tonnes of relief material on seven aircraft to Nepal till now.
"In addition to the relief material, we have also sent 54 personnel to support relief and rescue efforts in Nepal. This comprises 30 tunnel rescue experts, 19 forensic experts, and a five-member medical team. Our rescue and forensic teams are deployed on the ground, and they are working closely with the Nepalese authorities," he said.
The first tranche of relief materials was sent by India hours after Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke to his Nepalese counterpart Balendra Shah on August 26, the day the flash floods struck the Himalayan nation.
Mr. Modi had assured Mr. Shah of all possible humanitarian assistance to deal with the situation.
The floods have damaged 35 motorable bridges, 45 suspension bridges, and 40 km of black-topped roads, mainly in central Nepal, according to local authorities.
Mr. Jaiswal said India responded promptly to the flash floods in Nepal and will continue to support the reconstruction and recovery efforts in the country.
Published - September 05, 2026 06:35 am IST

stories.headline: Good news for car enthusiasts! Kia launches Sorento in India
stories.bodyText: Bengaluru: Carmaker Kia India on Friday launched the Sorento in the country, marking its entry into the premium three-row SUV space. The new vehicle is priced from Rs 27.99 lakh for the diesel version and Rs 29.49 lakh for the hybrid (ex-showroom)..The Sorento is Kia India’s first hybrid offering and is available in 6- and 7-seat configurations. The 1.6-litre turbo GDI hybrid combines an engine producing 180 PS and 265 Nm with a 65 PS electric motor delivering 264 Nm. It is paired with a 6-speed automatic transmission. The 2.2-litre diesel produces 193 PS and 442 Nm and comes with an 8-speed dual-clutch transmission..Both powertrains are available with all-wheel drive, with Kia describing the hybrid-AWD combination as a first in the segment. The SUV also gets Snow, Sand and Mud terrain modes..Built at Kia’s Anantapur facility in Andhra Pradesh, the Sorento measures 4,815 mm in length and 1,900 mm in width. Safety features include up to 10 airbags and 30 ADAS Level 2+ features..Bengaluru Airport’s new 'Care by BLR' plan: Bags picked up at home, chauffeur to KIA'.The India-spec Sorento also marks the global debut of Kia AI Assistant with real-time generative AI capabilities. The system can provide real-time information, respond to follow-up questions and control select vehicle functions..“The arrival of the Kia Sorento represents a defining milestone in Kia India’s journey as we enter the premium three-row SUV for the first time,” said Gwanggu Lee, MD and CEO, Kia India..Deliveries of the Sorento have already commenced nationwide.

stories.headline: Carlsen, Anish, Vidit, Divya Deshmukh, K Humpy in one team: How GCL made it possible
stories.deck: How did the Alpine APL Pipers assemble a dream team featuring Magnus Carlsen, Anish Giri, Vidit Gujrathi, Koneru Humpy, Divya Deshmukh and Volodar Murzin? Coach Pravin Thipsay reveals the strategy behind navigating the GCL draft, balancing star power with depth, and preparing for opponents’ recent rapid form. As defending champions, the Pipers must also manage expectations, media attention and…
stories.bodyText:
Magnus Carlsen
, Anish Giri, Vidit Gujrathi, Koneru Humpy, Divya Deshmukh, Volodar Murzin. Wait. This isn’t a draft for an all-star exhibition tournament, but the six-member roster that the Alpine APL Pipers have assembled to defend their Global Chess League (GCL) crown for Season 4 in Bengaluru.
If last season was about breaking the stranglehold of the Triveni Continental Kings to lift their maiden title, Season 4, starting this Saturday, is likely to be about something far more terrifying for the rest of the field.
Pairing World No. 1 Magnus Carlsen alongside positional titans Anish and Vidit, backed by the veteran grit of Humpy, FIDE Women's World Cup winner Divya, and former World Rapid Champion Murzin on the prodigy board, the Pipers have crafted what might be the most formidable franchise lineup ever placed on the battlefield of 64 squares.
But how do you assemble a modern-day Dream Team under a strict draft system where every single team enters the bidding room with identical resources?
How can someone build a team like that?
Pipers' coach Pravin Thipsay believes that constructing a squad of this calibre isn't about collecting shiny names.
"It's not a sort of building a star-studded lineup," Thipsay told TimesofIndia.com during an exclusive interaction, dismissing the notion that the roster came together by accident.
"It's important to have strong players since it's a double round-robin for qualification to the top two spots, and then it's going to be a one-to-one match. So there are two phases. We should have a team which is very good at beating some of the teams so that we finish in the top two, and in the second phase, once we end up in the top two, it's important to beat the other teams."
In a franchise ecosystem, every team starts with an identical bank of draft points.
Securing an Icon board like Magnus Carlsen, who returns to lead the Pipers after skipping last season, requires an immediate, massive financial outlay. The moment you go big on the top board, your remaining purse is instantly squeezed, forcing coaches into high-wire balancing acts for the Superstar and Prodigy boards.
“The best parameter in judging strength or the present strength of a player is the Elo rating, and that's the reason why I personally try to have the strongest rated players in my team,” Thipsay admitted.
“Now, the process of the draft is quite clear, and everybody starts with an equal number of points. How you spend those points in selecting the players, that is important.”
In reality, every coach walks into the venue eyeing the exact same elite names on each tier.
“Very often you have to spend most of your points on one or two players, and that leaves you in a tricky situation where you have lesser points, and you may not always get the best player you want,” the 67-year-old veteran Grandmaster added. “Nobody gets all the six players of their choice because others also aim for those players. So somewhere you have to see the balance. If you are able to get three of the most wanted or most coveted players in your team, I think it's a good team to start with. It's a tricky procedure to outmanoeuvre the other coaches. It's much trickier than what it appears to be.”
By securing Giri and Vidit to flank Carlsen on the top boards, while locking in Humpy, Divya Deshmukh, and Murzin, who offers incredible fast-chess firepower as a former World Rapid Champion, the Pipers managed to pull off the ultimate draft sweep across every single board category.
Behind the champion’s burden
Carrying the title of defending champions only heightens the target on their backs. Coach Thipsay knows that pretty well.
“The most important thing is, as defending champions, we should not be overconfident,” Thipsay told this website with some palpable firmness. “And we should not be again very attentive to the media. As a defending champion, the media is going to approach us more frequently than the other teams. But the most important factor in the game of chess is your preparation, your practice, your rest on that day.”
Pipers clinched the title last season (GCL Photo)
To combat the attention that inevitably surrounds a squad featuring Carlsen, Giri, and rising elite talents, Thipsay has already mapped out a strict operational barrier for the tournament.
“We are going to see that at no stage our players are losing their focus due to the media attention or anything else. So I am going to restrict the promotional activities to short tenures, very often after the games,” he revealed.
The prep of defending champions
Over the last few weeks, Thipsay has put his efforts into focusing heavily on the current form of his players rather than relying on their classical reputations.
“It's important to prepare once we know who is playing whom,” Thipsay acknowledged. “The board order was disclosed, so we started personally preparing against those opponents. The Icon board would prepare against all the Icons, and so on. I personally look at the games of these players and shortcomings in their recent games. I focus on finding out shortcomings of the opponents in their recent rapid games, not the classical ones. So that is my strategy.”
Is nothing going to stop Pipers then?
With the preliminary double round-robin kicking off at The Lalit Ashok Bangalore, the major challenge for the Pipers is perhaps more of a psychological nature. The underdog plays with uninhibited freedom, while the favourite carries the weight of the result.
"It's general public psychology and, of course, player psychology that opponents do better against the defending champions or against a stronger team," Thipsay reflected.
"The opposition which we are going to face could be more fierce, more prepared, and more motivated when playing with us, simply because there is an opportunity to beat the defending champions.”
Mitigating that threat for Thipsay means continuously reminding his superstar roster that past titles and Elo ratings offer zero safety once the clock starts ticking.
“We have to take into account that the same opponents may not be so strong against other teams, but they could be strong against our team,” he warned. “The second challenge I see is that the fact that we won in the third season doesn't mean that we're going to win the fourth season. Our team will have to be careful about any overconfidence that comes from results in preliminaries or earlier tournaments. Every game is a different one, and how you played yesterday has no bearing over how you are going to play today.
”
As the clock ticks down to Round 1 in Bengaluru, the Alpine APL Pipers stand on the precipice of GCL history. On paper, they have constructed a masterpiece. On the board, the hard work begins all over again.
“At the moment, we are well poised,” Thipsay concluded with trademark calmness. “The immediate goal is simple: finish in the top two in the preliminaries. Because after the preliminaries, there is no option. You have to try to be the champion.”

briefs.headline: Karnataka signs MoU with Australia-based INQ Innovation Global to connect startups with New South Wales technology
briefs.deck: State-INQ Innovation Global MoU to connect startups with New South Wales
briefs.bodyText: Bengaluru: Karnataka has signed an MoU with Australia-based INQ Innovation Global Pty Ltd to connect its startups with New South Wales’ technology and innovation ecosystem..The partnership will support market access, investor and industry linkages, research collaboration and cooperation in emerging technologies..The MoU was signed by the Department of Electronics, IT and Biotechnology, Government of Karnataka, and INQ Innovation Global, in the presence of IT-BT Minister Priyank Kharge, Irfan Malik, CEO and MD, INQ Innovation, and others. The partnership will create pathways for the state’s startups to access Australian markets, investors, industry networks and innovation ecosystems..It will provide mentorship, market-entry support and connections with companies, investors, institutions and government..An initial cohort of Karnataka startups is expected to explore the Australian ecosystem in the next phase..RDPR dept jobs 'scam': HD Kumaraswamy wants Priyank Kharge to resign.The collaboration will focus on DeepTech and AI, health and MedTech, agricultural and clean technology, biotechnology and life sciences, defence and aerospace..Other areas include quantum computing, digital infrastructure, AVGC-XR and gaming, digital health, precision agriculture, clean energy and advanced materials..The initiative will also connect universities, research institutions, companies and startups in Karnataka and New South Wales, supporting joint research, skill development and research commercialisation. The partnership will strengthen investor and venture capital links through introductions, deal-flow sharing, investor roundtables and pitch events..“Karnataka’s next phase of growth will be defined by how effectively we connect our startups, innovators and research institutions to global markets and capital,” Kharge said.

briefs.headline: ‘Even my wife is watching’: Srikkanth says Sooryavanshi is making cricket exciting
briefs.deck: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, only 15, is creating a stir in cricket circles. His skill has been showcased in the Duleep Trophy and IPL, alongside impressive international outings. Recently, he made Duleep Trophy history by breaking the 57-year-old record for the youngest half-century scorer. The BCCI is closely tracking his progress, with many experts predicting he could evolve into a cricketing icon on…
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Former India opener 
Kris Srikkanth
 believes Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has the potential to become one of the biggest names in world cricket, with the teenage sensation already generating an unusual level of excitement around the game.
Sooryavanshi, just 15, has continued his rapid rise by making a mark in the Duleep Trophy after already setting the IPL and international stages alight. For Srikkanth, however, the youngster's impact is going beyond numbers — he is making people tune in to cricket they might otherwise have overlooked.
“He's playing outstandingly well. He must be encouraged and never be discouraged. If he's moulded properly, he'll be a superstar in the making. He'll bring Test cricket back to its glory. Everyone watched the Duleep Trophy because of him. Even my wife is watching because of him. He'll be a big asset going forward for World cricket,” Srikkanth said on his YouTube channel.
‘He’ll be a superstar in the making’
Sooryavanshi has certainly given fans plenty to watch. After failing to make an impact in East Zone's quarterfinal win over North East Zone, he responded emphatically against Central Zone in the semifinal.
The teenager smashed 92 off 81 balls in the first innings and then contributed a crucial 40 in the final innings as East Zone secured a four-wicket victory to book their place in the final.
At 15 years and 157 days, Sooryavanshi had already become the youngest batter to score a half-century in Duleep Trophy history, breaking a 57-year-old record.
Srikkanth was particularly impressed by the teenager's fearless approach in red-ball cricket and believes there is little reason to question his ability to make the jump to the highest level.
“He played incredibly well. How can people even doubt whether this boy on whether he is capable of playing higher-level cricket? He can play every level of cricket, and he is going to rule world cricket shortly in all formats. He's smashing medium pacers with no worries for straight sixes in red-ball cricket. He's toying with the bowlers,” he said.
From IPL sensation to India star
Sooryavanshi's rise has been extraordinary. His breakthrough IPL 2026 campaign with 
Rajasthan Royals
 saw him score 776 runs in 16 matches at a staggering strike rate of 237.30, including a century and five fifties. His 72 sixes were an IPL record for a single season, while he collected the Orange Cap, Most Valuable Player, Emerging Player, Super Striker and Super Sixes awards.
He subsequently became India's youngest men's international debutant during the T20I series against England. Against Zimbabwe, he scored 151 runs in three matches to help India complete a 3-0 sweep and collected his maiden Player of the Series award.
His impact has also extended to age-group cricket. Earlier this year, Sooryavanshi amassed 439 runs at the ICC Under-19 World Cup and was named Player of the Tournament.
The 
BCCI
 is now taking a cautious, long-term approach to his development. Secretary Devajit Saikia said the board is monitoring the teenager closely and wants his early success to translate into a career similar to those of India's past legends.
“We want Vaibhav Sooryavanshi or any player of his stature to continue and serve like Sachin Tendulkar did for the country or other players who in the past became legends,” Saikia said.
“So we look at Vaibhav in a very serious manner. He's monitored from every angle and every step he is taking forward in his international career. The BCCI is taking a very close look at his future.”
The board's priority, Saikia stressed, is to ensure Sooryavanshi's emergence is not merely a brief burst of teenage brilliance.
“You see, the BCCI can be proud that we are promoting a player of the age of 15 years who is already making his mark in the international scenario and we are very cautious that every right step he should take forward so that it should not be a one series or one year wonder,” he said.
For now, though, Srikkanth sees something even bigger taking shape — a youngster whose fearless cricket is making people sit up and watch.

briefs.headline: Air pollution, biofilms and the lung
briefs.deck: Air pollution, biofilms and the lung
briefs.bodyText: By Mohana S Sundaram and Monica Medappa.Bengaluru’s worsening air quality was a major concern during the final months of 2025, with AQI levels reaching around 150–180. A study led by Professor Kasturi Mukhopadhyay at Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) found high levels of antibiotic-resistant bacteria in Delhi’s polluted air. The study raises concerns that polluted air may not only harm the lungs but also carry resistant bacteria into them..Prolonged exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5) can alter the respiratory microbiome and weaken the lung’s natural defences, creating conditions that may favour persistent infections. This can worsen chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), while long-term exposure to PM2.5 is also associated with lung cancer risk. COPD affects over 55 million people in India, and many of them are non-smokers. Pulmonologists link this to long-term exposure to outdoor pollution, biomass fuel smoke, workplace dust and traffic emissions..Polluted air may help bacteria persist.Research suggests that air pollution can alter microbial communities in the environment and favour bacteria that tolerate stressful conditions. Environmental stress can also activate bacterial responses that help microbes survive and persist. PM2.5 particles can carry microorganisms and other biological material deeper into the respiratory tract. Researchers are now examining whether these conditions could help some microbes persist in the lungs and form biofilms..Vehicular emissions major contributor to nitrogen dioxide pollution in Bengaluru: KSPCB .A biofilm is a community of bacteria that sticks to a surface or to other bacteria and becomes enclosed in a protective matrix produced by the microbes themselves. In the airways, damaged tissue and impaired clearance may make it easier for opportunistic bacteria to persist and form these communities..Biofilms contain a protective matrix of sugars, proteins and DNA that can make it harder for the immune system and antibiotics to reach the bacteria. Some microbes within biofilms can enter dormant states, making them particularly difficult to eliminate and allowing infections to recur..In COPD patients, persistent bacterial colonisation is associated with ongoing inflammation and recurrent exacerbations. Several bacteria linked to respiratory disease, including Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, can form biofilms..Dr Ajay Kalanjana Monnappa, CEO of BioSustain Labs at the Bangalore Bioinnovation Centre, explains that biofilms are difficult to target because once bacteria are embedded in the extracellular matrix, antibiotics may struggle to reach the biofilm’s inner core. Dormant microbes within the biofilm can also be more resistant to antibiotics. His research on bacterial biofilms, including Pseudomonas species, shows that bacteria communicate within biofilms through quorum sensing and can exchange resistance genes through horizontal gene transfer. As a result, prolonged antibiotic treatment may not eliminate all microbes within biofilms, allowing infection to recur after therapy ends..Clinical evidence on drug resistance.Research within India highlights the challenge of biofilm-associated drug resistance, although studies specifically examining COPD patients remain scarce. A 2015 study led by Saroj Golia at a tertiary care hospital in Bangalore found that 49.45% of clinical Staphylococci isolates could form biofilms. Biofilm formation was much more common among drug-resistant strains, with 75.32% of methicillin-resistant strains forming biofilms, compared with 30.47% of methicillin-sensitive strains. The data showed a strong association between biofilm production and multidrug resistance, with biofilm-forming strains showing complete resistance to erythromycin (100%) and high resistance to clindamycin (76.66%) and ciprofloxacin (70%)..Although the study did not examine pollution or COPD specifically, it illustrates the broader relationship between biofilm formation and antibiotic resistance..Nationally, a 2026 systematic review published in Cureus examined biofilm-associated antibiotic resistance among Indian clinical isolates of Klebsiella pneumoniae, a multidrug-resistant pathogen. The review found that strong biofilm-producing strains showed significantly higher resistance to carbapenems, which are used as a last-line treatment for some antibiotic-resistant infections. These strains were also resistant to 12 other antibiotic classes, including polymyxins..Long-term infection and inflammation may contribute to the relationship between COPD and lung cancer, but whether lung biofilms play a role in this link remains unclear..The biofilm-cancer connection.Researchers are investigating whether changes in the lung microbiome could influence lung cancer development. COPD increases the risk of lung cancer, while exposure to PM2.5 is associated with inflammation, oxidative stress and tissue damage..Prof. Mamatha Ballal, Head of Enteric Diseases at Kasturba Medical College (KMC), Manipal, explains that COPD may contribute to lung cancer through long-term inflammation and changes in the lungs and immune system. She also says that COPD and lung cancer are now closely linked worldwide because they frequently coexist, posing a major challenge for precision medicine..Recent oncology research has identified bacterial communities within tumour microenvironments. Scientists are investigating whether these microbial populations can influence inflammation, immune responses and tumour behaviour. How much this contributes specifically to lung cancer progression remains unclear..Prof. Ballal believes that “managing the link between COPD and lung cancer will require more than just standard medicines”. She highlights the potential of microbiome-based markers to identify higher-risk patients, while treatments that target the lung microbiome, along with inhaled therapies and better lung care, could help “slow disease progression and improve patient outcomes.”.Dr Monnappa, whose research at Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology in Korea focused on biological approaches to biofilms, says future anti-biofilm treatment will likely combine enzymes, quorum-sensing inhibitors, bio-based therapeutics and microbiome modulation rather than depend on a single therapy. His research on Gram-negative bacteria has shown that bio-based treatments can limit biofilm formation and reduce bacteria’s ability to invade human cells, with minimal toxicity to healthy cells. He adds that such treatments could enhance the effects of existing antibiotics and selectively target harmful bacteria without disturbing beneficial microbes in the body..For now, researchers see reducing exposure to pollution, early diagnosis and better management of chronic lung disease as the most established priorities. Microbiome profiling and biofilm-targeting therapies remain promising areas of investigation. Combining environmental data with microbial genomics could eventually help doctors detect respiratory problems earlier..(Mohana Sundaram S has a PhD in Regenerative Medicine from MAHE, and Monica Medappa is a PhD holder in Biomedical Sciences from Masaryk University, Czech Republic)

briefs.headline: Punjab government to hike DA of 85,000 employees from 42 to 60 pc: Minister Aman Arora
briefs.bodyText:
Chandigarh, Punjab government will raise the Dearness Allowance of around 85,000 government employees recruited after July 17, 2020 by 18 per cent to 60 per cent, Cabinet Minister Aman Arora said on Friday.
Speaking to mediapersons here, Arora said a recommendation in this regard was made by the Cabinet Sub-Committee formed to examine the issues of employees.
The announcement is significant as employees recruited after July 17, 2020 were getting a pay equivalent to the Central pay scales, along with 42 per cent Dearness Allowance (DA). These were much lower than the pay scales of employees recruited before July 2020, who were paid as per the Punjab Pay Commission.
Arora said there were two pay scales in Punjab, which was leading to conflicting interests and confusion: the Punjab basic pay scales and the one equivalent to the Central basic pay scales (as per the 7th Central Pay Commission).
"Punjab basic pay scales, which traditionally are higher, range from 30 to 70 per cent more than the Central basic pay. And when DA is added to it, which is currently 42 per cent, the salary increases much above the Central pay scales," he said.
"When we calculate and compare, even with 60 per cent DA added to Central basic pay, the Punjab pay scales and take-home salaries are higher," he said.
Arora said the previous Congress government had decided to hire employees on the Central pay scales after July 17, 2020.
In the last six years, 85,000 employees have been recruited.
The Mann government will give them a "Janmashtami gift" as the three-member Cabinet Sub-Committee has decided that the DA of these employees will be raised from 42 to 60 per cent. The committee's recommendation will be sent to the chief minister, Arora said.
He, however, said that this hike will not benefit employees recruited before July 2020.
"From day one, the Bhagwant Mann government has been talking about the welfare of every section. We cannot imagine good governance without our employees," he said.

briefs.headline: BRICS: Building, bridging and balancing
briefs.bodyText: Next weekend, the spotlight will be on the New Delhi BRICS 2026 summit. Leaders from BRICS nations will assemble to celebrate the group’s economic progress and endorse a political and financial architecture for a future-oriented agenda. BRICS’ priority from the outset was to promote practical collaboration for economic growth and development, collaborate with multilateral development banks, reform global governance and not oppose any group or country. That idea became a movement, spreading to the Global South. When India assumed the chairship of BRICS last January, BRICS was already the principal driver of global economic growth. It had overtaken the G7 in terms of GDP, was expected to surpass it in trade flows, was a major contributor to global manufacturing, was an emerging power in finance and technology, and had acquired greater heft with new members and partners. .BRICS 2026 | India's bilateral diplomacy confronts strategic fault lines.There were headwinds, too. Western narratives branded the group as an anti-West forum that would promote de-dollarisation. Then came the war between Iran, on one side, and Israel and the United States, on the other. Could India provide a steady hand to guide BRICS’ transition from aspiring emerging economies to impactful emerging powers? India's BRICS 2026 agenda maintained its focus on economic growth and global governance, while managing narratives and expectations. BRICS and economic delivery India framed the BRICS 2026 agenda on the theme of building for resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability. This thematic reorientation reflected the priorities of the current era, with people-centric and pragmatic outcomes. Through 350 convenings on political-security issues, economic engagement and civil society exchanges, India built all-round consensus to take BRICS confidently into its third decade. The extent of intra-BRICS economic cooperation is often not well known to the public. Yet, it is these outcomes that have had a profound impact on the lives of citizens, are the principal reason for its popularity and explain why many countries seek membership. Over the last 20 years, BRICS has collated an economic database of key areas of cooperation, potential projects, partner institutions and established working mechanisms. Today, with BRICS, especially India, growing faster than the global average, the capacity and capability to deliver are even greater. Some of the key economic and social outcomes during BRICS 2026 are worth enumerating. BRICS built synergies through a network focused on digital agriculture and genetic agro-research, created a digital ecosystem for MSME cooperation, supported skilling cooperation and developed a global value chain plan. Its economic partnership strategy designed an efficient logistics supply-chain framework, while, on energy security, framed standards for smart grids and energy storage. Recognising the importance of technology and innovation, it established an incubator network, a start-up innovation fund and a science and research repository. Similarly, there were citizen-focused endeavours in health, wellness, climate change and other sectors. Perhaps one of the most far-reaching developments is expected in the financial architecture for cross-boundary transactions. Starting in 2014, well before the narrative of de-dollarisation was born, BRICS began to facilitate local-currency trade and finance through its New Development Bank, interlinked systems for financial settlements, and the use of central bank digital currencies in coordination with central banks; these mechanisms provided faster, cheaper and more transparent transactions. They will not replace existing dollar mechanisms but supplement them, adding efficiency and resilience. BRICS also held political-security consultations and deliberations on the reform of multilateralism and the new global order. Admittedly, these were not easy issues and the endeavour for convergence demanded ever greater efforts. BRICS and the Iran war The war involving Iran, Israel and the United States was a challenge to BRICS. Two non-BRICS countries, Israel and the US, attacked a BRICS member, Iran, which retaliated with attacks against their assets in the region and missile and drone strikes on several Gulf countries, including BRICS members, the UAE and Saudi Arabia. The prolonged war had devastating consequences for the regional and global economy, energy security, supply chains and the power balance in the region. It pitched BRICS members on opposite sides in the conflict and was a matter of concern, even while all were aware that any solution lay beyond the BRICS realm. BRICS sought an end to hostilities and convergence within the group. BRICS Sherpas responded with urgency and maturity and met on multiple occasions. They highlighted the need for peace and stability in the region and for maintaining freedom of movement for energy and other resources, but the war had its own dynamics. The BRICS deputy foreign ministers discussed the issue of West Asia in April but could not reach consensus, owing to divisions between the UAE and Iran. When the foreign ministers met in May, the gap in views between the two sides on the war was yet to be bridged, but the chair’s statement reflected the overarching consensus on every other agenda issue and recorded that there were diverse perspectives on one issue. This pragmatic approach brought home the fact that diplomatic parleys do not always yield convergence and that even this realisation is an outcome, although it is not a solution. It was an exercise in expectations management through high-stakes diplomacy. As India prepares for the summit, BRICS is expected to maintain its call for diplomatic negotiations, an end to hostilities, and peace and stability in the region. The expectations-management exercise, initiated earlier, has brought better awareness to all sides. Conflict has become the currency of leverage, while diplomacy has fallen a step behind in West Asia. Indeed, that is part of the strategy of the belligerents, even while they haven’t forsaken diplomacy. In a wider perspective, BRICS needs to consider building crisis-management capacities to deal with future scenarios that are likely to witness frequent conflict, rising protectionism and growing fragmentation amid new uncertainties. Over the last two decades, BRICS has shown agility and success in maintaining its development focus while members grew as emerging economies. India’s chairship has prepared BRICS with greater capacity and capability for the coming decade of geoeconomic opportunities and geopolitical uncertainty, when members may also act as emerging powers with global responsibility while seeking global governance. .(The writer is a former BRICS Sherpa and currently a professor at Jindal Global University)

briefs.headline: Kyrgyzstan signals shared roads for SCO
briefs.deck: Bishkek signals shared roads for SCO
briefs.bodyText: The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO)’s two-day summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, was notable for the united positions it projected in spite of the diverse political, economic, and security interests of the constituent members. The Bishkek Declaration reflected shared interests arising from a sense of territorial contiguity and an awareness of common challenges and possibilities. Its condemnation of the United States-Israel war on Iran is significant, not only for the support it extends to Iran, a member of the group, but also for its strong messaging against the Donald Trump administration. India joining the other members in this position is an important development. Members strongly criticised Western sanctions that violated the United Nations Charter. The Declaration also underlined the rights of all countries to pursue peaceful nuclear programmes..At the summit, members chose a broadly accommodative approach on some of the polarising issues. The Declaration expressed the grouping’s commitment to fight terrorism, including cross-border transgressions. This reflected Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s call to dismantle terror infrastructure and end double standards in handling the issue. His words were aimed at Pakistan, which signed the declaration after Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif noted that his country, too, was a victim of terrorism. The summit underlined the role of China as the leader of the Global South and an evolving multipolar world. President Xi Jinping called upon the member states to support multilateralism and contribute towards reforming global governance. Xi’s words and China’s positions are seen as providing direction to a world order that has a diminished role for the US. These developments align with China’s continuing efforts to shape a yuan-based international system and Russia’s moves to de-dollarise trade..PM Modi, Kyrgyz Prez reaffirm commitment to further strengthening Strategic Partnership.Since its origins as a security-oriented organisation, the SCO has widened its scope, now covering economic cooperation, trade, and infrastructure. The Bishkek Declaration has called for industrial cooperation and the development of transport corridors, multimodal connectivity, digital commerce, and national currency settlements. The idea of a transport corridor connecting South Asia to Europe through Central Asia has immense potential. India’s continuing focus on the Central Asian region draws on economic and security objectives. Before attending the summit, Modi visited Uzbekistan, where an agreement was firmed up for the long-term supply of uranium and critical minerals to India. The two countries have upgraded their ties to a strategic partnership and expanded their trade and economic relations. India’s increasing engagement with the SCO members marks an important turn in the shifting geopolitical environment.

briefs.headline: Real growth, beyond branding
briefs.bodyText: NITI Aayog’s suggestion that Karnataka develop a “second Bengaluru” to ease the growing pressure on the state capital deserves serious consideration. It comes at a time when Bengaluru’s success is constraining its future. The state government’s decision to prepare a plan in response is welcome, but the exercise must go beyond identifying another satellite suburb. Bengaluru has grown from a relatively compact city of about 40 lakh people in 1991 into a sprawling metropolitan region of more than 1.3 crore people. The municipal footprint expanded from just 69 sq km in the mid-20th century to 226 sq km by 1995, and now exceeds 710 sq km under the Greater Bengaluru framework. Roads, public transport, water supply, drainage, and other civic infrastructure are under relentless pressure. Traffic congestion, water scarcity, groundwater depletion, and the loss of green spaces are now structural challenges. Simply extending the city’s administrative or economic boundaries cannot resolve them..NITI Aayog asks Karnataka to build second Bengaluru.The urgency is greater because Karnataka and Bengaluru are among India’s principal growth engines. The GSDP for 2025-26 was Rs 32.81 lakh crore, with growth at 8.1%. Services contribute nearly 70% of GSDP, reflecting the extraordinary concentration of technology, startups, finance, research, and global businesses in Bengaluru. The city’s success has benefited the entire country, but excessive concentration is neither sustainable nor desirable. The government’s policy of rebranding neighbouring areas as Bengaluru’s extensions is therefore misplaced. Renaming Ramanagara as Bengaluru South or proposing Bengaluru North for Tumakuru may create a stronger real-estate brand, but it does not build a new economic centre. Such measures risk encouraging speculative development, longer commutes, and greater pressure on the capital’s infrastructure..A “second Bengaluru” should ideally be a tier-2 city with a salubrious climate, established educational institutions, good connectivity and, crucially, an operational airport. Belagavi and Shivamogga merit consideration, among others. The objective should be to set up a complete economic ecosystem – technology, manufacturing, research, education, and services – rather than another residential township. The Centre, however, must do more than offer policy advice; it should provide targeted capital grants, viability-gap funding, and concessional financing for transport, digital infrastructure, industrial parks, water, and urban services in the chosen growth centre. The aim should not be to create another Bengaluru in size, but to replicate its opportunity. Such a growth centre would ease pressure on the capital while spreading Karnataka’s prosperity more evenly. NITI Aayog has identified the problem; the Centre and the state must now turn the suggestion into a funded, time-bound project.

stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 The

 Association of Unaided School Managements (KAMS) has urged the state govt to resolve technical issues plaguing the Student Achievement Tracking System (SATS) within seven days and immediately stop what it termed “pressure, intimidation and harassment” of school staff over pending online work.

stories.headline: With 4.5k e-buses, over 50% Bengaluru Metropolitan Transport Corporation’s fleet set to be electric in 18 months
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru: More than half of BMTC’s fleet could be electric within 18 months, with the state cabinet Thursday approving induction of 4,500 e-buses under the Centre’s PM E-DRIVE scheme.
The addition, combined with replacement of ageing vehicles, is expected to expand BMTC’s fleet from around 7,000 buses to nearly 11,000 in 18 months. BMTC operates 1,700 e-buses under the gross cost contract (GCC) model.
The Centre will provide the 4,500 buses, while the State will extend Rs 600 crore annually to BMTC as viability gap funding. BMTC is, however, expected to face an annual shortfall of around Rs 1,000 crore in operating the expanded electric fleet and will have to meet the remaining gap through its own resources.
Union minister for heavy industries HD Kumaraswamy told 
TOI
: “Bengaluru is growing rapidly. To strengthen the city’s public transport system, the Centre has made the highest allocation of buses under the PM E-DRIVE scheme. The induction of 4,500 e-buses will help reduce congestion and provide environmental benefits. The Centre is ready to provide more e-buses if BMTC requires them.”
Under the GCC model, private operators will supply and run buses, while BMTC will pay them on a per-kilometre basis. 
The 4,500 buses will include 3,500 non-air-conditioned 12-metre buses, 300 air-conditioned 12-metre buses, 600 non-air-conditioned nine-metre buses and 100 air-conditioned nine-metre buses.
Once agreements are finalised, the first batch of buses is expected to arrive in six months, with the entire fleet inducted over the following year. BMTC currently retires around 500 to 600 old buses annually.
Earlier assessments by BMTC had indicated that the cost of operating e-buses under GCC could exceed the revenue generated, prompting it to seek assistance. The Rs 600-crore fund is expected to bridge part of the deficit.
The Centre had completed the tender process in Dec 2025, but the state took several months to approve BMTC’s participation in the central scheme amid concerns over financial implications and operational efficiency.
Transport minister Byrathi Suresh said the govt had decided to raise Rs 2,000 crore from the Centre to strengthen transport infrastructure across Karnataka, including construction of new depots and upgrading bus stands.
He said more than 1 crore women would shortly receive smart cards under the Shakti scheme, with the first phase expected to cost around Rs 250 crore.
++++++
WHAT BMTC PAYS
* Rs 62 per km for 12-metre non-AC buses, Rs 55 for nine-metre buses
* Rs 70 per km for AC buses under likely 12-year contracts
* Buses to run 200km a day
* BMTC to recruit more conductors, plan 30 to 35 depots to operate and maintain new fleet
* Will provide conductors and handle ticketing
+++++
Bus fare revision soon
On a possible fare revision, transport minister Byrathi Suresh said fuel prices had increased four times in eight months. A committee headed by retired IAS officer Atul Tiwari is expected to submit its report shortly. Bus fares, he said, would be increased marginally without placing an additional burden on the public.

stories.headline: Three held after woman alleges abduction, assault over debt in Bengaluru
stories.deck: The accused also allegedly stripped her and recorded a video, according to the FIR. However, the police are verifying the claims.
stories.bodyText:
The Bengaluru police have arrested three people, including two women, after a 30-year-old woman alleged that she was forcibly taken to a house, assaulted, and held captive for two days by the accused over an alleged debt. She was rescued by the Chandra Layout police after a credible tip-off.
The accused also allegedly stripped her and recorded a video, according to the FIR. However, the police are verifying the claims. The accused have been identified as Nazrath Begum, Reshma Banu, and Suhail.
According to the FIR, the victim had borrowed ₹50,000 from Nazrath on a weekly-interest arrangement and had also borrowed ₹1 lakh from Reshma about two years ago. She said that she had been paying ₹5,000 every week to Nazrath, but had been unable to make payments for about two weeks. For the ₹1 lakh loan from Reshma, she had not paid interest for six months.
The woman alleged that Reshma had been repeatedly demanding money and threatening her. She claimed that she eventually moved to her mother’s house fearing harassment and later stayed at another friend’s house.
On August 27, the complainant said Nazrath called her to the latter’s house offering to pay her some money. After she arrived with her son, Reshma, her husband Suhail, and two other men allegedly entered the house and locked the door.
The complainant told the police that Suhail demanded the money back and allegedly assaulted her. The woman further alleged that she and her son were forcibly taken in an autorickshaw to Reshma’s house in Kumbalgodu, where she was allegedly assaulted with a stick and was subsequently kept confined in a room. The assault continued the next day as well.
The victim also alleged that Nazrath stripped her and recorded a video on the latter’s mobile phone, threatening to circulate it if she failed to repay the money. The woman said she was later taken to a lawyer near a market and made to sign some papers before being brought back to Reshma’s house.
On August 31, she managed to get out of the room when she was allowed to use the toilet. Police personnel arrived at the house shortly afterwards and rescued her. She was taken to the Chandra Layout police station, where she narrated the alleged incidents.
Based on the complaint, the Chandra Layout police registered an FIR against under relevant sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and the Information Technology Act.
An investigator in the case said that the accused and the victim are all friends and a financial dispute is involved. “We are verifying all the claims made by the complainant,” the officer told The Hindu.

stories.headline: Tempers fly, traffic crawls as vehicle restrictions kick in on Bengaluru airport road
stories.deck: The Bengaluru Traffic Police (BTP) began enforcing its recent announcement of a ban on certain categories of vehicles on four elevated corridors in the city on Friday, with only the Airport Road flyover seeing a ban on two-wheelers
stories.bodyText:
Traffic on airport road near Sanjeevininagar Cross in north Bengaluru crawled on Friday during peak hours, while motorists hurled abuses at traffic police personnel who were at the spot to enforce the ban on certain categories of vehicles, including two-wheelers, on the elevated corridor.
The Bengaluru Traffic Police (BTP) enforced its announcement of a ban on certain categories of vehicles on four elevated corridors in the city on Friday, with only the airport road flyover seeing a ban on two-wheelers.
Chaos ensued on airport road, with the congestion extending for nearly a kilometre, while the other three flyovers — BGS, Peenya, and Double Decker — saw effective enforcement, resulting in considerable traffic disruption.
Enraged commuters
At each flyover, at least 10 police personnel were deployed to divert restricted vehicles from entering the flyover. They stood at both edges of the entrances to the elevated corridors, carrying batons with blinking red lights.
Although heavy vehicles and autorickshaws were restricted, two-wheeler riders maneuvered through the gaps between heavy vehicles and evaded police restrictions, entering the flyover.
“It is deadly for both our officers and the motorists if we try to stop them, because a lot of vehicles commute along the stretch; even one fall could turn fatal. We refrained from strict enforcement but diverted 50% of two-wheelers who were driving on the sides of the road,” an officer at the field told The Hindu.
When riders commuting along the sides of the road were asked to move to the service lanes, they stopped and questioned the traffic personnel about the many two-wheelers entering the flyover.
Long queues
As the traffic police started imposing a no-entry restriction on goods vehicles and autorickshaws, they stopped them in the middle of the road, which meant slowing down traffic.
However, the disruption was not significant along the service lanes, which saw seamless movement of vehicles. But for the officers, it was a long day at work as they worked in three-hour shifts alternately from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m.
An officer said: “Commuters have to be familiarised about the diversions for some days; hence, we also didn’t expect 100% enforcement. But when strict enforcement is taken up, we will start booking cases.”
In addition, the elevated corridors have AI-equipped cameras through which cases will be booked for flouting “no-entry” rules, which attract a penalty of ₹500.
While the BTP has backed the move of restrictions by citing accident data that shows 15 fatal accidents on the KIA elevated corridor stretch in 19 months, two-wheeler riders questioned whether banning them was the only way to curb accidents.
Nakul S., a resident of Yelahanka, questioned whether the BTP was running a pilot to turn all flyovers in the city into corridors exclusively for cars and buses. “It is the police’s job to shape lane discipline among commuters, which they have failed to do. There are ways to curb haphazard driving with advanced traffic technologies, which should be explored, rather than keeping two-wheelers away from roads citing safety,” he said.

briefs.bodyText:
On other city flyovers, traffic police enforce restrictions on goods vehicles and autorickshaws
