Traffic on the Peenya Flyover along Tumkur Road in Bengaluru on Friday following a partial relaxation of restrictions on two-wheelers. Autorickshaws and heavy vehicles continue to be prohibited from using the flyover.
Traffic police are taking a graded approach while imposing restrictions on the movement of two-wheelers, autorickshaws and goods vehicles on the city’s key flyovers: Electronics City, KIA flyover, Peenya, and BGS-Sirsi Circle flyover.
The ban came into force on Friday, but the level of enforcement was uneven. While police actively diverted other restricted vehicles at Silk Board and BGS, they took a lenient approach towards two-wheelers on the KIA corridor and Peenya.
Here’s a lowdown on what 
Team TOI found on Day One.
KIA Flyover: 6km ban, endless woes for motorists
Ban applies to a 6km stretch from Esteem Mall and Vidyashilp Junction, and not the entire KIA expressway. Display boards have been placed at entry points on both sides of the banned section where two-wheelers, autorickshaws and goods vehicles do not have entry.
Near Esteem Mall, the southern entry point of the restricted stretch, three traffic policemen were stationed. Two-wheelers continued to enter the flyover.
“Today is the first day… We’re looking after mostly VIP movement,” a traffic policeman said. Some riders were unsure whether to use the elevated route. 
Sajeev KS, a commuter, chose the road below. “I saw many bikers still using the flyover, but I didn’t take the stretch as I was wary of cameras,” he said.
In the afternoon, 
TOI found that the journey towards Vidyashilp through at-grade road took 11 minutes, as much of the traffic, including two-wheelers, was still using the flyover. The reverse journey took 18 minutes, with four signals along the route and an increased presence of goods vehicles diverted from the elevated stretch.
A commuter travelling towards Yelahanka said morning traffic was bumper-to-bumper on the service road between the upper ramp near Kodigehalli Junction and GKVK, taking him nearly 20 minutes to cover the stretch. Another rider said traffic towards the airport was unusually congested between the Kodigehalli downramp and Baptist Hospital in the afternoon.
Police said enforcement against two-wheelers would be tightened gradually. A senior officer said 1.5 lakh vehicles use KIA elevated corridor daily and stopping two-wheelers moving in the middle or right lanes could pose safety concerns.
“If the two-wheelers come on the extreme left lane, we can stop them, but they are using the extreme right lane or middle lane, so it was difficult to stop them considering their safety and traffic movement,” the officer said, adding that enforcement could take another 2-3 days.
Another officer said police were ensuring that goods vehicles did not enter the airport road flyover, while the two-wheeler restriction would take time to enforce.
Peenya: Stricter ban, per-km fatigue increases
On the 4.5-km Sri Shivakumara Swamiji Flyover at Peenya, police enforced restrictions strictly, stopping passenger autorickshaws and three-wheeler goods vehicles at barricades placed at Peenya and Chikkabidarakallu ends — but they were lenient towards two-wheelers. Heavy and medium goods vehicles are barred during peak hours, between 7am and 11am and 4pm and 10pm.
Autorickshaw drivers questioned the need for the ban, saying relatively few autos used the flyover but those undertaking longer trips depended on it to bypass junctions such as 8th Mile and Jalahalli Cross. Prakash, an auto driver, said a 20-minute journey from Yeshwanthpur to Anchepalya could take nearly an hour on the road below.
Silk Board: Goods vehicles carry ban load
At Silk Board, police diverted heavy goods vehicles to the at-grade road after barring them from the double-decker flyover between Ragigudda and Silk Board.
BGS: No big impact, cargo vehicles face barricades
At the BGS Flyover, heavy goods vehicles have been banned round-the-clock, while light and medium goods vehicles are barred between 7am and 11am and 4pm and 10pm. Police said the restriction had not significantly affected traffic since vehicles were routinely diverted during periods of congestion.
++++
‘Last Ride’ Shifts To Low Gear, Cops Rev Up KIA CampaignBengaluru: Hours after superbike riders were stopped from heading to KIA for their “last ride” early Thursday, Devanahalli police increased barricades and launched awareness efforts on flyover restrictions.
Police counselled riders on traffic rules, safe and responsible riding. Only around 40 superbikes passed through the checkpoint and proceeded further from late Thursday night.
A senior officer said the bikers had caused “a nuisance” by blocking the flyover on airport road. They had misinterpreted that two-wheelers were banned on the entire KIA expressway, while the ban is only from Kodigehalli Junction to Vidyashilp Junction, about 6km.
Close to 400 bikers had come for what they declared the “last ride”. They took the upper ramp of the flyover, which connects from Begur Road. “We had expected the bikers to come again on Thursday night. However, their numbers were not large. We educated them about accidents and traffic jams caused by autorickshaws and goods vehicle breakdowns and sent them away,” a senior officer said.

briefs.headline: Bengaluru woman choked, robbed of gold chain worth Rs 9 lakh
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: A 55-year-old farmer was robbed of her gold mangalya chain, weighing around 85 grams and worth nearly Rs 9 lakh, after an unidentified man grabbed her by the neck from behind. The incident took place around 4.30pm Wednesday in Hosahalli village near Hunasamaranahalli in northeast Bengaluru.
According to the complaint filed by Lakshmidevamma, she was plucking flowers near her neighbour Venkataswamappa’s house when the miscreant allegedly attacked her. The accused then fled on a two-wheeler parked nearby. The victim described him as a man aged around 35, with a heavy build, wearing a black T-shirt, a backpack and a helmet.
The stolen chain included two mangalya pieces, two gold bullets, and a pendant. The incident took place hours after a miscreant grabbed gold mangalya chains from two women at their house in Kadusonnappanahalli. Bagalur police have registered both cases. A senior officer suspects that the same person committed both crimes.

briefs.headline: New trains to give Bengaluru Metro chance to overhaul fleet
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 Every 
Namma Metro
 train covers an average of 450 to 500km a day, and eight six-coach trainsets have now clocked nearly 10 lakh km of operations. With four new trainsets for Green Line expected to enter service soon, operator BMRCL will have an opportunity to undertake major mid-life maintenance of its older rolling stock.
BMRCL has received CMRS (Commissioner of Metro Rail Safety) approval to use the new rolling stock for passenger services.
The corporation currently operates 57 six-coach trainsets on the Purple and Green Lines. During peak hours, 33 trains operate on the Purple Line and 22 on the Green Line, with an average frequency of around 3.3 minutes and five minutes, respectively. During non-peak hours, a few trains are withdrawn for scheduled maintenance.
An official said maintenance schedules are prescribed by the manufacturers for every one lakh, five lakh, and 10 lakh kilometres. “About 50 coaches have now crossed 10 lakh km of operations,” he said.
BMRCL currently operates 469 round-trips across Purple, Green and Yellow Lines. Of these, Purple Line accounts for 186 trips, Green Line 160, and Yellow Line 123.
Asked whether the induction of new trains would improve peak-hour frequency, the official said BMRCL was examining the issue. 
“We’re working on it now and will inform about the frequency. We’ll redraw the timetable,” he said.
However, he pointed out that there were limitations to increasing frequency, including dwell time — the duration a train remains stationary at a station platform to allow passengers to board and alight. “We can’t drastically squeeze the dwell time because people are involved. We’ll see how best we can induct more trains to ease congestion,” he said.
The new trains will also give BMRCL greater operational flexibility to withdraw older trainsets for major maintenance. “Till now, we’ve been hard-pressed to take out Metro trains for major maintenance. With the induction of new trains, we’ll get an opportunity to carry out these works,” the official said.
BMRCL began commercial Namma Metro operations with the opening of a 7km stretch between Byappanahalli and MG Road. The network has since expanded to 96km, with services operating on Purple, Green and Yellow Lines. Initially, BMRCL operated three-coach trains before introducing six-coach services in 2020, when the network had expanded to 42km.
BOX2 trainsets a month
The general life of a Metro trainset is around 35 years, a Metro official said, adding that the planned work could be considered mid-life maintenance. “This will improve the efficiency of the trains,” he said. Maintenance requirements vary because the trainsets entered service in different years.
A BMRCL press release stated that of 21 trainsets, four have been received and will be progressively introduced into revenue service, while the remaining 17 are expected to be delivered regularly at the rate of two a month.

briefs.headline: 5 inmates assault, try to strangle prison officer in Bengaluru
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 A warder at Central Prison, Parappana Agrahara, was attacked by five prisoners arrested in the activist Suhas Shetty murder case. The prisoners allegedly assaulted him, dragged him into a room and attempted to kill him by strangling him.
According to a complaint filed by Manjunath HG, superintendent in-charge of Central Prison, the incident occurred around 10.45am on Sept 2.
The injured warder, Manjunath Haveli, 32, works in the Shiksha Bandi section, which handles premature release cases. He had gone to Annex-1 jail building at 10.05am to collect information about a prisoner ahead of a videoconference scheduled for 11.30am.
While there, undertrial prisoner Mohammed Musamir allegedly confronted Haveli over an earlier incident on Aug 22, when Musamir was transferred from the security division to the Annex-1 jail building and was stopped from taking additional items inside the prison.
Musamir allegedly threatened Haveli before punching him in the face and nose, causing him to bleed. Four other prisoners — Abdul Safwan, Mohammed Rizwan, Nayaz and Kalandar Shafi — then allegedly joined the assault.
The five prisoners are said to have dragged Haveli into room no. 4 and continued attacking him. They also squeezed his neck tightly and attempted to suffocate him. Other prison staff present at the spot intervened and rescued Haveli.
Based on the complaint, Parappana Agrahara police have registered a case under various BNS sections, including attempt to murder. A senior officer said the accused were questioned Friday evening and taken into police custody after obtaining court permission.
The accused were arrested by the National Investigation Agency (NIA) following Shetty’s murder near Bajpe in Mangaluru on May 1, 2025. NIA has arrested 12 accused and filed a chargesheet against them.

briefs.headline: Expired chilli, artificial colours found at Sahakaranagar club in Bengaluru; kitchen seized
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: The Food safety wing of the department of Food Safety and Drug Administration (FDA) conducted a special inspection at Chairman’s Club in Sahakaranagar (Dollars Colony) Thursday.
Officials found 40kg of expired chilli stored as a food product. They also found 5kg of breadcrumbs and 2kg of Sajeera food products with improper labelling that did not comply with Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) regulations.
The inspection also revealed highly unhygienic conditions in the food preparation and storage areas, along with the use or storage of unauthorised/prohibited artificial colours in food products. The club was not following prescribed food-safety measures for the storage and handling of food items.
Another violation flagged by the inspection team was the storage of vegetarian and non-vegetarian food products together. Alleging serious deficiencies, officials closed and seized the club kitchen and initiated legal action.
Notices issued to 23 PGs
Following multiple complaints, a special investigation drive was conducted at paying guest (PG) accommodations across the city Friday and notices were issued to 23 PGs for alleged hygiene lapses.
During the drive, officials inspected 64 PGs, collected a total of 12 food samples and sent for laboratory analysis.
Items like expired curd, bisibelebath powder, rice flour, synthetic food colour, black pepper and misbranded mixture were seized.
At Nandana Elite PG in Bommasandra, officials found bed-bug powder kept on the dining table along with food articles. Unused and non-food-related materials were also found stored in an area where drinking water facilities were provided. Following the observations, the department sealed the dining area.
Vidhana Soudha found clean
The food safety department inspected the pantry of the Cabinet Hall at Vidhana Soudha during a cabinet meeting Thursday at 11am. The department said no problems were found and everything was found well-maintained.
Officials checked the cleanliness and sanitation of the pantry. Under food storage and labelling, officials verified whether all food items were clearly labelled with their manufacturing and expiry dates. The inspection also covered pest and waste control, including checks for signs of pests, rodents and droppings.

briefs.headline: Specialist-doc can’t sit idle over no govt postings: Karnataka high court
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: Karnataka high court has observed that a qualified super-specialty doctor is not expected to remain idle when govt doesn’t provide any posting in spite of requests, adding that it’s an unacceptable proposition that a doctor doing a super-specialty course must remain indebted to the govt for the rest of his official life.
A bench comprising Justices Anu Sivaraman and Venkatesh Naik T made the observation, disposing of appeals filed by Bangalore Medical College and Research Institute and medical education department. Consequently, the civil-contempt petition filed by cancer specialist Dr Adnan Saeed was disposed of.
Dr Saeed secured a seat in Kidwai Memorial Institute of Oncology (KMIO) to pursue Masters in surgical oncology under the in-service quota. He executed a bond on his deputation from BMCRI and joined KMIO on Aug 31, 2015. He completed the three-year course in 2018 and was relieved from deputation on Aug 8, 2018.
He sought a posting at KMIO since there were no surgical oncology positions at BMCRI. He waited for three years and quit in Aug 2021.
On April 11, 2022, BMCRI refused to accept his resignation and directed Dr Saeed to report to duty. Despite his detailed explanation, a domestic inquiry was ordered against him in Oct 2022 over unauthorised absence.
He moved the high court against the proceedings. On April 5, 2023, a single bench quashed notices and directed the chief secretary to pay salary to him for the period for which no posting was given.
BMCRI and medical education dept contended Dr Saeed failed to honour the bond and chose to work abroad. The division bench noted, “In the absence of posting orders, appellants cannot raise contentions (of him going abroad) in these proceedings.”

briefs.headline: Anganwadi workers’ deployment of booth-level officers challenged in Karnataka HC
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 Karnataka high court Thursday issued notice to the 
Election Commission of India
 (ECI), chief electoral officer of Karnataka, and the state govt on a petition challenging the appointment and deployment of 
anganwadi workers
 as booth-level officers (BLOs) during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
The PIL was filed by Karnataka State Anganwadi Workers and Helpers Union, state committee, Davanagere.
A division bench of Chief Justice Vibhu Bakhru and Justice KS Hemalekha, after a brief hearing, directed the respondents to submit their responses and posted the matter for further consideration on Dec 1.
The petitioners cited ECI guidelines issued on June 5, 2025, which stated that BLOs should first be appointed from among regular Group C and above employees of the state govt or local authorities.
According to the union, anganwadi workers should be considered for BLO duties only as a fallback when eligible regular employees are unavailable and after following the required non-availability certificate procedure.
The petitioners said anganwadi workers already perform several essential public-welfare duties, including early childhood care and education, providing supplementary nutrition, assisting pregnant women and lactating mothers, conducting home visits, and monitoring malnourished children. 
They argued that routinely assigning them election-related duties could affect these critical services and interfere with their primary responsibilities.
The petitioners said regular govt or local-authority employees should be considered for BLO duties first, with anganwadi workers deployed only in exceptional circumstances, after the non-availability of eligible regular employees is properly established.

briefs.headline: Bengaluru woman takes money for 2 years, attacks lover with iron object
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 A two-year relationship built on repeated promises of marriage took a violent turn as a 33-year-old man accused his lover of attacking him with an iron object following a heated argument at her west Bengaluru home.
According to a complaint filed by 
Sagar
 (name changed), a tattoo artist, he had known private firm employee 
Sujatha
 (name changed) for around two years, and they fell in love. He alleged that she had repeatedly promised to marry him, often saying she would marry him “tomorrow”, while gradually taking money from him.
Sagar said he called Sujatha multiple times on Sept 2, but she did not answer. He subsequently went to her home at Gollarahatti, where he allegedly saw her having an “obscene” conversation with another man over a video call.
An argument reportedly broke out between them when Sagar questioned her. He alleged that Sujatha attacked him with a heavy iron object from the kitchen. As he tried to flee, she struck him again on the head and forehead, leaving him seriously injured.
Sagar said he managed to escape and reached a private hospital nearby, where he received treatment.
Expressing fear that Sujatha and her family members could threaten or attack him again, he urged police to provide him protection.
Byadarahalli police issued a notice to the accused.

stories.headline: HUL plans capex boost; eyes entry into new areas
stories.bodyText:
MUMBAI: After two years of sluggish growth, Hindustan Unilever (HUL) is stepping up investments to defend market share amid stiff competition from a clutch of new-age brands and changing shopping patterns. On Friday, the consumer goods giant said that it will boost capex to 3% of turnover from 2% in the last five years and "decisively" enter select high growth spaces.
In its presentation to investors on Capital Markets Day, the company said that it will bet on the emerging pockets of consumption to drive expansion-a strategy the firm has dubbed internally as 'winning in new India.' "Structural shifts in new India present an attractive FMCG growth opportunity," HUL said.
Last year, HUL replaced former CEO Rohit Jawa, passing on the baton to another company insider Priya Nair. Under Nair, the firm has been sharpening focus on consumer approach, crafting different strategies for different consumer classes. In a category like hair care for instance, growth in rural areas will come from increased consumption and premiumisation while in big urban cities, addition of new products to haircare routine and increased penetration will boost demand, the company said.
"HUL will leverage its iconic portfolio to unlock competitive volume-led growth through consumption, premiumisation, market making and entering new spaces," the maker of Knorr soups and Dove shampoos said.
HUL has spent on new-age brand acquisitions bringing D2C startups such as Minimalist to its fold and is stepping up focus on distribution through quick commerce channels as consumers increasingly take to instant delivery of groceries and other household staples. In the June quarter, HUL posted an underlying sales growth of 10%, delivering its highest growth in 13 quarters. HUL's share price ended at Rs 1,974 apiece on the BSE on Friday, up 0.9%.

stories.headline: Discretionary spending by households rose in FY25
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: As the economy recovered from covid pandemic, household spending in 2024-25 marked a further shift towards non-essential discretionary items and services, which have earlier seen decline, signalling premiumisation and a boost for govt revenues.
After seeing a decline in 2023-24, growth in household spending on alcoholic beverages, tobacco and narcotics (22.4%) outpaced growth in all other item categories to Rs 2.7 lakh crore, nearly double than what households spent on 'recreation, sport and culture' (Rs 1.4 lakh crore), the latest national accounts data released by NSO, with the revised base year 2022-23, showed.
Similarly, the 'personal care, social protection and miscellaneous goods and services' category, which has seen spending decline in 2023-24, saw a rise of 19% to Rs 5.3 lakh crore.
Jewellery items, such as precious stones, wristwatches, smartwatches etc are covered under this category, along with personal care items like electric razors, hair trimmers, deodorants, sun glasses and grooming services, such as tattoo clubs, salons, spas and saunas. Travel goods like back packs and personal items like lighters, satchels and hand bags are also covered.
Though the total private final consumption expenditure (PFCE) in real terms increased nearly 6% to Rs 169 lakh crore in 2024-25 - a pace similar to the previous financial year, much of this rise was cornered by services sector as share of spending on services of the total PFCE rose to 45.2% (Rs 76.3 lakh crore) as compared to 44.4% (Rs 70.5 lakh crore) previously.
Among services, other categories like 'insurance and financial services' saw a 10% jump in spending to Rs 11.4 lakh crore and health saw 9% rise to Rs 8.7 lakh crore.
Among essential categories, spending on food items increased 4% to Rs 45.5 lakh crore, with growth in spending on sugary products (11%), ready made food items (9%) and protein rich items like milk & dairy products, fish and seafood (nearly 7 %) outpacing cereals, eggs, fruits and vegetables. Non alcoholic beverages like soft drinks, water and juice also saw robust growth (25%) in spending in 2024-25.

stories.headline: A BIT of a reset, with a wider debate
stories.deck: Revising India’s bilateral investment treaty (BIT) requires consultation and stronger democratic accountability
stories.bodyText:
It has been widely reported that India is revising its model bilateral investment treaty (BIT) and that the revised text will soon be placed before the Union cabinet. The seeds of this were sown when Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said in the Union Budget speech in 2025, that India was considering revamping its 2015 Model BIT. The treaty was adopted as part of a broader appraisal process launched after several foreign investors sued India for BIT breaches. The two key outcomes of this appraisal were the unilateral termination of BITs and the adoption of a new model BIT as the basis to launch new negotiations.
A model that is out of balance
In the last decade or so, India has managed to conclude only a handful of BITs based on its 2015 model. This reveals the many limitations of the 2015 model, which many scholars, including this writer, have repeatedly pointed out. If investment treaties aim to balance the two competing objectives of investment protection (one end of the spectrum) and the state’s right to regulate (the other end), the Indian model BIT tilts heavily towards the latter. This creates doubts among countries that export capital to India about the legal protection afforded to their investments. These doubts are exacerbated by high regulatory risks, not-so-well-developed governance models, and an agonisingly tardy judicial system. As these concerns have grown louder, India has rightly decided to revisit the model, apparently with the objective of pulling the pendulum back towards the centre.
Any process of review of BITs has two core components. The first is on what substantive and procedural changes need to be made to the law; and the second is about what processes need to be followed to ensure the robustness of the outcome. The first aspect has attracted considerable attention, with experts pointing out the necessary legal reforms, such as making it easier for foreign investors to use international arbitration for treaty claims, enhancing the substantive protections for foreign investment, and having more investment facilitation measures. However, the second issue has not been deliberated much.
Concerns about democratic deficit
Since international economic treaties, including those on foreign investment, have a conspicuous impact on citizens, it brings into play the all-affected principle in democracy. In other words, whether those affected by, say, an investment treaty should have a right to participate in decision-making. If those affected are not able to participate effectively in decision-making, say, through their elected representatives or other civil society organisations, it raises concerns about ‘democratic deficit’ in the treaty-making process. Originating in debates in Europe, ‘democratic deficit’ refers to the insufficient oversight of technocrats and bureaucracies, or the executive in general, including the political executive, who negotiate and evolve treaty frameworks behind closed doors. The lack of oversight may take many forms, such as a lack of or inadequate parliamentary supervision of the treaty-making process, and an absence of an external consultative process with other stakeholders, including subject-matter experts and civil society organisations.
To overcome the charge of ‘democratic deficit’, many countries, such as the United Kingdom and Australia, mandatorily place the text of the negotiated treaty before ratification on the floor of the Parliament, enabling it to express its views. Specifically, in the context of model BITs, Norway held two rounds of public consultations — in 2008 and 2015 — on an updated draft. Likewise, Colombia released its model BIT for public consultation. India, too, in March 2015, circulated its draft 2015 model BIT for public comment. This provided an opportunity for the Law Commission of India (LCI) to assemble a team of experts to study the draft model BIT. The LCI, in its 260th report, made recommendations on how to improve the draft model BIT. India finally adopted the revised version in December 2015, though not all of the LCI’s recommended changes were reflected in it.
Have a consultative process
Presumably, the government must have already undertaken widespread internal consultations, i.e., intra-governmental deliberations on the model BIT. As regards external consultation, the following may be considered. First, form a core team of experts, external to the government, who have demonstrated proficiency in international investment law or foreign investment, and engage with them. This would ideally include international lawyers and economists drawn from universities, research institutions and think tanks. This core team could act as the sounding board for the government. Second, invite industry bodies, arbitrators, law firms, and other civil society organisations to offer their views on the model BIT.
Following these first two steps, the third step will be to prepare a draft and place it in the public domain, inviting comments from the public at large, as done in March 2015. In the fourth step, or simultaneously, the draft model BIT should be placed on the floor of Parliament for discussion. The relevant department-related parliamentary committees can also be roped in for the same. Most notably, this consultative process should not be carried out merely as a box-ticking exercise, but as a meaningful activity that upholds the spirit of participatory democracy, which would necessarily include engagement with dissenting views.
Prabhash Ranjan is Professor and Vice Dean (Research), Jindal Global Law School, and was part of the team of experts assembled by the Law Commission of India to study the 2015 draft model bilateral investment treaty (BIT)

stories.headline: Coal stock management emerges as key challenge for thermal power producers
stories.deck: India may not need a complete overhaul of its coal-allocation policy, but it must stress on sharper implementation, and fixing accountability on power producers who may not be adhering to the stipulated norms for maintaining adequate coal inventory.
stories.bodyText:
India’s thermal power sector faces a growing fuel-management dilemma with generators that maintain adequate coal inventories risk being disadvantaged when limited domestic supplies are redirected to plants that fall below prescribed stock norms.
While such emergency interventions may be necessary to keep vulnerable plants operational and safeguard grid reliability, industry stakeholders warn that repeated redistribution could undermine incentives for generators to plan and maintain adequate fuel stocks.
Coal-stock requirements for thermal power plants have been in place for years. The current Central Electricity Authority (CEA) framework took effect on December 6, 2021, introducing revised, plant-specific stocking norms aimed at strengthening fuel security and inventory planning.
The broader coal-supply framework—including coal linkages, Fuel Supply Agreements (FSAs) and other supply arrangements—is intended to provide generators with greater certainty over fuel availability and allow them to plan inventories more effectively.
The revised SHAKTI policy, approved by the Central Government in May 2025, further streamlined coal-linkage allocation into two windows. Window I provides coal linkages to central government-owned generating companies and state utilities at notified prices, while Window II allows other eligible producers, including imported-coal-based plants, to procure coal through auctions at a premium over the notified price.
The Ministries of Coal, Power and Railways also coordinate regularly to monitor coal supplies and facilitate movement to power plants, particularly during periods of supply disruption, such as what emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic when all forms of transport came to a standstill, necessitating CEA’s revised coal supply framework.
Industry seeks differentiated approach
Emergency assistance to plants facing critically low stocks can be justified when consumer interests and grid stability are at risk. However, industry stakeholders argue that such support should distinguish between genuine supply-chain disruptions and persistent shortages caused by inventory mismanagement.
“Coal inventory should be recognised as a system reliability service, with generators maintaining adequate or higher-than-normative stocks appropriately incentivised, while repeated shortfalls without genuine external causes should carry consequences,” said Rajib Mishra, former Managing Director of PTC India, earlier known as Power Trading Corporation of India.
Mr. Mishra said coal availability at the mine does not automatically translate into fuel availability at a power plant. Fuel security depends on the entire logistics chain, including production, loading, railway availability, transit, unloading and stockyard management.
Emergency redistribution, he said, should therefore be reserved for genuine supply-chain disruptions such as mine-side constraints, railway bottlenecks, force-majeure events or unexpected spikes in electricity demand.
Aggregate supply not the only concern
India’s coal production exceeded 1 billion tonnes in each of the last two financial years, reaching 1,047.52 million tonnes (MT) in FY2024-25 and 1,040.08 MT in FY2025-26.
In the current financial year, cumulative production through July stood at 302.04 MT, while overall coal dispatches rose about 6% year-on-year to 354.7 MT.
Government data showed coal stocks at thermal power plants at 34.55 MT, with another 113 MT either at pitheads or in transit. The combined stock was therefore around 148 MT.
The figures indicate that the challenge is not necessarily a shortage of coal at the national level, but how efficiently supplies are allocated, transported and converted into adequate plant-level inventories.
Thermal power remains critical to grid security
The issue has gained importance as electricity demand continues to rise and thermal generation remains central to meeting peak requirements.
Coal- and lignite-based plants, with around 230.8 GW of installed capacity, accounted for 69.54% of electricity supplied during April-June 2026. During non-solar peak hours, thermal generation reached about 188.8 GW, or nearly 75% of total generation.
Peak power demand touched 270.2 GW in May.
“CEA monitoring has shown differences in plant-level inventories, making fuel management an important part of India’s energy-security framework,” an industry official said, eeking anonimty.
Legal framework also favours equitable treatment
The issue also has a legal dimension. In its September 2025 judgment in Haryana Power Purchase Centre & Others v. GMR Kamalanga Energy Ltd., the Supreme Court rejected claims by individual distribution companies seeking preferential access based on the dates of their Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) or the stated source of coal.
The court held that additional costs arising from the use of costlier coal should be shared equitably among procurers.
The developments suggest that India may not require another major overhaul of its coal-allocation architecture. Instead, the immediate priority could be stronger implementation of existing norms, greater accountability and differentiated treatment of generators based on their inventory-management performance.
Plants facing genuine and demonstrable supply disruptions should receive timely assistance. At the same time, persistent stock shortfalls without credible external causes should trigger a clearly defined corrective mechanism, an executive from a large power producer said, adding the policy challenge is increasingly to ensure that emergency coal redistribution protects grid reliability without turning prudent fuel management into a commercial disadvantage.

briefs.headline: As protein demand rises, brands go for smaller packs
briefs.bodyText:
Mumbai: Protein foods are now a common sight across retail shelves, but consumers may increasingly also have the choice to go for smaller-sized portions going ahead. As protein-deficient Indians become picky in terms of what they eat and add to their regular diets, companies are pushing smaller and more affordable protein packs into the market to widen consumption.
From breakfast smoothies to wafers, bars and snacks-brands are making protein foods more convenient and accessible. And it's not just limited to specialised protein products; firms are also packaging foods that are naturally rich in protein in smaller sizes. ITC, for instance, recently launched chana sattu in eastern regions starting at Rs 10, which offers 10 grams of protein per pack, also tapping into regional nuances.
"Protein intake is not just about the quantity consumed, but also about making it easier to include protein at different consumption occasions during the day. Smaller, convenient packs can help consumers add protein across meals or while snacking rather than relying on one or two meals alone," said Hemant Malik, executive director at ITC.
Consumption of protein foods today is not just limited to households that are economically well-off. 
A recent study by Worldpanel by Numerator showed that the lower affluent class is opting for a range of healthy snacks and beverages (including some protein snacks and drinks) for on-the-go consumption.
"Small-format packs can play an important role in making protein a more accessible part of everyday snacking. For consumers who are new to the category, a smaller pack lowers the entry barrier, making it easier to try, understand and eventually build a habit around protein-led products. It also fits naturally into today's on-the-go consumption occasions, whether that's a quick snack between meals, at work or while travelling," said Aditi Jain, head of brand & marketing at D2C brand SuperYou, which has introduced protein wafers and puffs across single and multi-serve packs within Rs 50. Tarun Arora, CEO at Zydus Wellness, which earlier this year expanded its range of protein snacks by adding a new millet wafer protein bar, said that today there is greater consumer scrutiny of ingredients and growing interest in protein. A 40-gram pack of the bar is priced within Rs 70.
Parag Milk Foods is also widening its smaller protein snacking range with products priced at under Rs 100. "Parag Milk Foods is approaching protein consumption across multiple consumption occasions, rather than treating protein purely as a sports-nutrition category," the company said. Smaller packs are the sweet spot for consumption, said Harsch Koshti, regional marketing director, IFF Taste for Greater Asia. "The protein trend is definitely here to stay and we will see more and more specialised nutrition products designed for specific target audience, occasions and applications," Koshti added.

briefs.headline: Unfinished agenda larger than I thought: Axis CEO
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Under Amitabh Chaudhry, who has headed Axis Bank for seven-and-a-half years, the bank delivered an 18% ROE for nearly seven quarters. However, the retail cycle, higher credit costs and rate cuts put pressure on NIMs. In an interview with TOI, Chaudhry spoke about how 18% ROE remains a target, though it is aspirational and difficult to achieve.
n You will be completing your third three-year term next year. What has been achieved and what is left to be done?
From strengthening the brand, improving net promoter score and upgrading businesses and subsidiaries, I am satisfied with what we have achieved. But the unfinished agenda is larger than I thought a few years ago: deeper penetration, premiumisation, consistent performance, stronger deposits and capitalising on AI. Execution remains critical. Covid and the retail cycle tested us along the way. We have moved ahead of competition in payments, with strong UPI and merchant-acquisition shares and a stronger credit card franchise after Citi acquisition. We have also built the third-largest wealth franchise in four years. Retail quality has improved but remains a work in progress.
Will you have to trade growth for margins?
It would be the wrong approach to say, "I can either fix growth or NIMs." 
We can do both. Our size is not yet so large that if I have to work too much on NIMs, I have to sacrifice something else. There are times when market dynamics or external factors could impact our margins, but in the medium-to-long term, we believe we can deliver 3.8% without too much of a problem.
Has Citi acquisition delivered?
It has delivered. The deposit/advance portfolios, synergies and talent benefits we expected have materialised. We also received an unexpected Rs 2,000-2,300 crore tax benefit, effectively lowering the acquisition price. It strengthened our credit card and wealth franchises and added deposits when they were becoming a constraint. Given the effort required even for a small acquisition, we now believe acquisitions should be big enough to justify that effort.
So you are open to growing inorganically?
We are always open. We have never shied away from it. The right one needs to come along at the right price. If you look at our size, HDFC is more than double ours. We are a decent franchise with a great set of customers. If the right one comes along, we will look at it.
Do you think banks have missed the bus on UPI?
When people discuss UPI market share, they focus on front-end apps; banks provide the rails. Every transaction relies on banks for authorisation, funding, fraud checks, disputes, regulatory liability and customer money. Apps spent heavily to acquire customers when UPI launched, then leveraged that base to build other businesses. MDR (merchant fees) and transaction data give banks scope to underwrite, understand and reach customers better, creating a potential advantage. Axis has 35% share of the rails it provides and 20% as an issuer, making it a major player. MDR should help make UPI self-sustaining without charging consumers, while NPCI is adding more use cases to make the infrastructure more useful.
But customers who earlier did not need to visit banks because of mobile and internet banking now don't need to visit the app, because large payments can be made through UPI. How do you remain relevant?
UPI covers payments, but banking offers a far wider suite of services. With MDR potentially creating revenue, banks will compete harder for payments, and we are well placed with our existing share. The same shift is happening in brokerage and mutual funds.

briefs.headline: Breather for India? Trump’s Russia sanctions bill may be stalled for now; could have led to 100% tariffs
briefs.deck: Lawmakers are concerned that the legislation could give President Donald Trump broader authority to impose tariffs and potentially push oil prices higher. Meanwhile, India’s reliance on Russian crude has increased sharply and is at record levels.
briefs.bodyText:
US President Donald Trump may not be able to get the Russia sanctions bill passed in the House of Representatives before November, a development that would give India a breather from the possibility of up to 100% tariffs for its crude oil purchases from Moscow.
The bill that received overwhelming support in the US Senate last month is facing increasing resistance in the House of Representatives and could remain stuck there until at least the November elections, according to a Bloomberg report.
Lawmakers are concerned that the legislation could give President Donald Trump broader authority to impose tariffs and potentially push oil prices higher.
The Russia Sanctions Bill
The opposition emerging among lawmakers from both parties is a boost for the retail sector and the influential business group US Chamber of Commerce. Both have raised concerns that the legislation could provide the Trump administration with additional legal grounds to impose tariffs on a much wider scale.
The legislation was introduced by the late South Carolina Senator Lindsey Graham, a strong supporter of Ukraine. It would allow Trump to impose tariffs of 100% on the five biggest buyers of Russian crude oil and natural gas, along with the five leading countries helping Russia circumvent energy sanctions. 
China, India and Turkey are currently the biggest buyers of Russian petroleum products.
Russia Sanctions Bill: What it means
Supporters of Ukraine in Washington have been advocating the bill as a means of demonstrating continued US backing for Kyiv. However, uncertainty remains over whether Trump would make use of the additional powers provided by the legislation, particularly when it comes to China, the Bloomberg report said.
The Senate approved the sanctions bill by a sweeping 86-11 vote. The strong backing was partly seen as a way for Graham’s fellow senators to pay tribute to him following his sudden death in July, shortly after he returned from a trip to Ukraine. The legislation has received a much less enthusiastic response in the House.
House Speaker Mike Johnson on Thursday indicated that the bill may not even be brought to the floor for a vote before the November 3 midterm congressional elections. One reason, he said, is that lawmakers are scheduled to spend only a limited number of days working in Washington over the next two months.
Johnson also pointed to opposition from the senior Democrats on the foreign affairs and tax-writing committees, saying this could signal wider problems in securing Democratic support. He added that there are also “pockets” of unease among House Republicans.
“We all believe in sanctioning Russia, but you have to have the right formula if you are passing a bill,” he told reporters Thursday. “We’re trying to work through that and make sure we can get a product that can get across the line.”
US oil prices in focus
House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said lawmakers are examining the bill partly to determine how it could affect gas prices. Mast, a Florida Republican, said forcing India and other purchasers of Russian crude to seek oil from alternative suppliers could put upward pressure on prices.
“That is part of what’s being evaluated right now,” he said.
Gasoline prices have surged following the Iran war and are increasingly seen as a potential liability for Republicans ahead of the November midterm elections, when the party will seek to retain its majorities in Congress. The legislation would also continue longstanding sanctions against Iran.
Democrats, meanwhile, are concerned that Trump could rely on the legislation as an additional legal basis for imposing broad tariffs, at a time when his existing tariff measures are already being challenged in court.
Representative Gregory Meeks, the senior Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said he could not back legislation that would give the president tariff powers “that he doesn’t have.” He also objected to a provision in the Senate-approved bill that would allow Trump to waive sanctions, arguing that the provision weakens the measure.
Representative Brad Schneider, another Democrat on the committee, also said the tariff provision could not be accepted.
“I’m not prepared to give any president, but in particular this president, more unfettered authority over tariffs,” he said.
If Johnson seeks to move the bill through an expedited House procedure, he would need substantial Democratic backing because the process requires a two-thirds majority. The speaker has recently found it difficult to get legislation approved through the regular process, as his narrow majority has left him vulnerable to opposition from members of his own party.
Business groups have also raised objections to the legislation. In August, a broad group of business lobbyists, including the Retail Industry Leaders Association, wrote to Congress outlining their concerns. The US Chamber of Commerce and the National Foreign Trade Council also joined the group. The latter represents trade-dependent companies including ExxonMobil Holdings Corp., General Electric Co., Ford Motor Co., and Pfizer Inc.
“We continue to remain concerned that a piece of the bill could have unintended consequences for consumers by authorizing new, expansive tariffs on other countries, who are our trading partners and allies,” Ellen Jackson, director of government affairs at the Retail Industry Leaders Association, said in a statement.
What it means for India
India’s reliance on Russian crude has increased sharply and is at record levels. Russia was not traditionally a major source of crude for India, but that changed after Moscow’s war with Ukraine began. As European buyers moved away from Russian oil, large volumes became available to India at steep discounts.
Russian oil shipments to India have risen consistently since 2022, with Russia accounting for more than 30% of India’s total crude imports for more than three years. The trend changed only in early 2026, when India’s purchases from Russia declined following the US sanctions imposed on Russian oil majors Lukoil and Rosneft.
However, that decline did not establish a lasting trend. The US-Iran war subsequently disrupted access to Middle Eastern oil, prompting India to increase its purchases from Russia. The US also temporarily waived sanctions on Russian crude during this period. Although that waiver has now expired, Indian refiners have continued buying Russian oil in substantial quantities, with imports reaching record levels in recent months.
Experts say Russian crude has effectively become the foundation of India’s crude procurement strategy.
Russia accounted for approximately 55% of India’s crude imports in July, its highest-ever share since India began making large-scale purchases of Russian oil after the Ukraine conflict. Russian crude continues to play an important role for India from the perspectives of both energy security and refinery economics.
India does, however, have a relatively diversified crude import basket, with more than 40 countries available as suppliers. It has also recently increased its purchases from Venezuela.
If Russian crude becomes commercially unviable, experts believe India could raise imports from Iraq, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, the US, West Africa, Brazil and Guyana.
But replacing the entire volume supplied by Russia would not be easy under current market conditions.
Experts view the Bill primarily as a tool to put pressure on countries continuing to purchase Russian oil.

briefs.headline: Chennai emerges as key development hub for Zoom’s Global Contact Center
briefs.deck: Zoom President of Product and Engineering Velchamy Sankarlingam says Chennai has a key role in developing the company’s Contact Center, while AI is reshaping the skills it needs to hire and the way its support workforce operates
briefs.bodyText:
Chennai has emerged as a key development hub for Zoom’s global Contact Center business, with teams in the city working on critical components of the cloud-based customer service platform, according to Velchamy Sankarlingam, President of Product and Engineering at Zoom.
While Zoom Contact Center is developed across multiple locations globally, India is the primary development base for certain components of the products, Sankarlingam said. He declined to disclose the specific areas being developed in Chennai.
“In terms of development, context and product, there are certain components, like India is the primary development,” he said, adding that Chennai has played a “big role” in product and contextual development.
Zoom established its Chennai technology centre in 2022, primarily focusing on product development. The company has increasingly positioned Contact Center as a key part of its broader strategy to expand beyond video conferencing into workplace collaboration and customer engagement.
Zoom Contact Center enables businesses to manage customer interactions across voice and chat, while also incorporating AI-powered virtual agents.
Enterprise business drives growth
Zoom does not disclose revenue separately for individual products, Sankarlingam said, when asked which of its enterprise offerings was generating the most revenue.
The company reported Enterprise revenue of $787.5 million for the quarter ended July 31, an increase of 7.8% from a year earlier. Enterprise revenue accounted for roughly 62% of Zoom’s total revenue of $1.28 billion. Online revenue stood at $489.7 million, up 0.6% year-on-year.
Zoom reported GAAP net profit of $1.54 billion for the quarter, boosted by a $1.61 billion gain from strategic investments. On a non-GAAP basis, net income was $464 million.
AI reshapes customer support
Sankarlingam said Zoom is also using its own Contact Center and AI capabilities internally, particularly in customer support.
The company is targeting a 40% reduction in support tickets, while AI and virtual agents currently handle more than 95% of incoming support tickets, he said.
According to Sankarlingam, the objective is not merely to automate customer interactions. Data generated through support conversations is being analysed to identify the root causes of customer problems and feed those insights back to product teams.
This allows Zoom to address underlying product issues before they result in additional customer complaints, while enabling human support agents to focus on more complex cases.
Demand shifts towards AI and business skills
The growing use of AI is also changing the type of talent Zoom is seeking.
Sankarlingam said the industry initially focused heavily on hiring professionals with deep artificial intelligence and machine-learning expertise. The requirement is now gradually shifting towards employees who can combine AI capabilities with an understanding of business processes.
However, he said the majority of Zoom’s current hiring continues to be concentrated in core AI capabilities.
To a query whether enterprises are primarily adopting AI-driven solutions to reduce headcount, Sankarlingam said companies are more focused on improving productivity and moving employees away from repetitive tasks towards more complex work, while creating new roles and skills.
Multi-model AI strategy
Zoom is taking a multi-model approach to AI, using a combination of its own models, open-source models and foundation models from companies including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.
Sankarlingam said the strategy enables Zoom to select models based on factors such as accuracy, performance and cost. A new capability could initially rely on a foundation model and later migrate to a Zoom-developed model as the company’s own technology improves.
The approach also helps the company manage token costs by selecting models that can deliver the required quality with fewer tokens, he said.
Hybrid infrastructure
Zoom operates a combination of public cloud infrastructure and co-located data centres. Its real-time audio, video, phone and Contact Center services generally run through its data-centre and global network infrastructure.
The company does not build or own its own data centres. Instead, it uses public cloud services and co-location partners, with approximately 18-20 co-located facilities globally, according to Sankarlingam.
In India, Zoom serves customers ranging from multinational corporations operating in the country to domestic businesses. The company has also modified some of its products to meet Indian regulatory and compliance requirements.

briefs.headline: NSE gets SEBI nod for ₹30,000 cr IPO; issue could be India’s second-largest
briefs.deck: The SEBI approval marks a key milestone in NSE’s long-delayed listing plans and brings the exchange closer to what could become one of India’s largest capital-market offerings.
briefs.bodyText:
The National Stock Exchange of India (NSE) has received regulatory approval to proceed with its proposed ₹30,000 crore initial public offering (IPO), potentially making it the second-largest IPO in India, after the proposed Jio Platforms listing.
The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has issued its letter of observation to NSE, clearing the exchange’s Draft Red Herring Prospectus (DRHP) for the public offering.
NSE had filed its DRHP on June 17, 2026, after its much-anticipated IPO was delayed for nearly a decade amid regulatory and legal-related overhangs.
The proposed IPO will be entirely an offer for sale (OFS), with existing shareholders looking to sell up to 14.89 crore equity shares, representing approximately 6% of NSE’s paid-up capital. The issue will not involve any fresh issuance of shares by the exchange.
Among the existing shareholders planning to offload their holdings, the SBI Group is expected to be the largest seller, offering up to 2.475 crore shares.
Other major shareholders participating in the OFS include MS Strategic (Mauritius) Ltd, which may sell up to 1.60 crore shares; Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPPIB), up to 1.19 crore shares; Aranda Investments (Mauritius) Pte Ltd, up to 1.12 crore shares; Bank of Baroda, around 1.10 crore shares; and Stock Holding Corporation of India Ltd, around 1.09 crore shares.
