briefs.headline: Neighbour held 4.27 acres for 40 years; 80 year old original owner gets his title restored
briefs.deck: Long-term occupation of a property does not automatically amount to adverse possession. To establish such a claim, there must also be a clear assertion of hostile title along with the necessary animus.
briefs.bodyText:
Your neighbour has possession of your land and after some years claims ownership of it on the basis of long possession. Is that legal? Karnataka High Court recently ruled on one such case.
The Karnataka High Court, relying on several Supreme Court precedents, has held that simply remaining in possession of a property for a long period, a legal concept referred to as adverse possession, does not by itself create ownership rights.
The court also made it clear that an incorrect entry of a person’s name in a particular column of land revenue records cannot establish title to the property.
What the adverse possession case is about
The ruling arose from a dispute over 4 acres 11 guntas of land in Sira Taluk of Tumakuru district. The case involved a neighbour who had remained in possession of the land for around 40 years and subsequently claimed ownership over it.
The original owner, Horakerappa, son of late Sanarangappa, had held the property since 1951. The land had been granted to him by the Assistant Commissioner, Madhugiri, through Order No.Dis.GD.10/51-52.
Horakerappa acquired the land in 1951 and continued to remain in possession of it thereafter, regularly paying kandayam, the fixed land tax or revenue.
The dispute began after Horakerappa’s neighbour, Eranna, sold his adjoining property to Thimmappa. After becoming Horakerappa’s neighbour, Thimmappa also began claiming rights over Horakerappa’s land.
Thimmappa’s family remained in possession of the disputed property for four decades. During this period, Thimmappa’s name was also entered in column 12 of the land revenue records through a mutation carried out by the revenue authorities.
Thimmappa therefore relied on two aspects of his claim: his family’s 40-year possession of the property and the presence of his name in column 12 of the revenue records. Horakerappa, however, did not accept the claim. At 80 years of age, he chose to fight the legal battle to protect his ownership of the 4 acre 11 guntas property, an ET report says.
The dispute escalated in the first week of August 2000, when Thimmappa allegedly attempted to take the land away from Horakerappa. Faced with this, Horakerappa approached the court seeking a declaration of his ownership and a permanent injunction restraining Thimmappa from interfering with his possession.
Horakerappa initially succeeded before the trial court, which granted both the declaration and injunction in his favour. Thimmappa challenged the decision before the first appellate court, which overturned the trial court’s ruling.
Horakerappa lost the case in appellate proceedings but won in High Court.
What Karnataka High Court ruled
The appellate court noted that Horakerappa had not produced the 1951 grant certificate as evidence. According to the court, the absence of this document raised a doubt over his title to the property. The revenue records containing Thimmappa’s name were also taken into consideration while deciding the appeal.
Horakerappa then challenged the appellate court’s decision before the Karnataka High Court. On August 7, 2026, the High Court ruled in his favour and restored the judgment of the trial court. The case was heard by Justice H.P Sandesh of the Karnataka High Court.
Significantly, the sale deed executed between Thimmappa and Eranna itself recognised Horakerappa as a neighbour and also referred to his boundary wall.
Despite this, Thimmappa’s name appeared in column number 12 of the land revenue records for the years 1972 to 1973 and 1981 to 1982 following a mutation carried out by the local revenue authorities.
Horakerappa disputed this entry, alleging that it had been made due to a mischief by the revenue authorities. Thimmappa relied on these entries to assert ownership over Horakerappa’s land and remained in possession of the property for 40 years.
The case ultimately became a battle over whether long possession and a revenue-record entry could displace the original owner’s title.
The Karnataka High Court ruled that occupying another person’s land without permission for more than 12 years is not, on its own, sufficient to claim adverse possession or ownership.
A person making such a claim has to establish before the court how the property came into his possession, produce evidence supporting his title and prove his case.
The High Court further clarified that an erroneous entry in revenue records cannot be treated as proof of ownership. This includes situations where a person’s name is entered into the records through a mutation carried out by revenue authorities for reasons that are not known.
Why did Horakerappa win the case in the Karnataka High Court?
- 40 years of possession alone was not enough: Long-term occupation of a property does not automatically amount to adverse possession. To establish such a claim, there must also be a clear assertion of hostile title along with the necessary animus. 
- The revenue record entry did not create a title: The fact that Thimmappa’s name appeared in Column No.12 of the RTC could not, by itself, establish ownership of the property. Horakerappa’s name continued to be recorded in Column No.9. 
- Thimmappa himself acknowledged Horakerappa’s 1951 grant: During cross-examination, Thimmappa admitted that Horakerappa had been allotted land in the original Sy.No.92 and that both parties had received land in that survey number. 
- The 1998 sale deed worked against Thimmappa’s claim: When Thimmappa purchased Eranna’s property in 1998, the sale deed described the boundaries in a manner that identified Horakerappa’s property.
- The absence of the original 1951 grant certificate did not defeat Horakerappa’s case: The original grant certificate was not available, but the evidence on record, particularly the admissions made by Thimmappa, was sufficient to establish that the grant had taken place.

briefs.headline: Phuket-Delhi flight incident: Air India terminates pilot who tested positive for drugs
briefs.deck: Air India terminated a pilot's employment after he tested positive for a psychoactive substance. This action followed an incident where the aircraft experienced multiple hydraulic failures. The flight encountered an altitude upset, causing injuries to passengers and crew. The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau recommended action against the pilot. A detailed investigation into the incident…
briefs.bodyText:
Air India on Friday said it had terminated the employment of the Pilot-in-Command of its Phuket-Delhi flight after he tested positive for a psychoactive substance.
“The Pilot-in-Command of the Phuket-Delhi flight tested positive for a psychoactive substance. In line with Air India's zero-tolerance approach to violations of safety, fitness or regulatory requirements, the pilot's employment has been terminated with immediate effect,” an Air India spokesperson said.
The action follows a preliminary report by the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) into an August 4 incident involving Air India flight AI-2379, which found the Pilot-in-Command's psychoactive substance test non-negative in confirmatory testing.
Pilot tested non-negative in confirmatory test
According to the AAIB's preliminary findings, both pilots underwent post-flight medical checks after the aircraft landed in Delhi. Their breath analyser tests were satisfactory.
However, the Pilot-in-Command's sample was found non-negative in a psychoactive substance detection test. A subsequent confirmatory blood test was also found non-negative, while the co-pilot tested negative.
The AAIB said the confirmation of the use of a psychoactive substance was a “serious concern” and recommended that the Directorate General of Civil Aviation take appropriate action on priority to prevent abuse of such substances.
The preliminary report did not establish that the substance finding caused the altitude upset. The detailed investigation into the technical and other aspects of the incident remains underway.
Multiple hydraulic failures during flight
The Airbus A320 was cruising at 36,000 feet when its flight-control system detected a loss of pressure in the green hydraulic system at 04:02:43 UTC, according to the AAIB preliminary report.
Four seconds later, the system detected losses in the blue and yellow hydraulic systems. The autopilot disengaged at 04:02:48 UTC, followed by a stall warning that lasted two seconds.
The co-pilot, who was the pilot flying, initially responded before the Pilot-in-Command took over the controls. During the altitude upset, the aircraft gained 372 feet and then fell 292 feet from its assigned flight level.
The blue hydraulic system recovered at around 04:02:52 UTC, followed shortly by the yellow and green systems, restoring the flight-control surfaces and returning the aircraft to normal operating condition.
Passengers and crew injured
The seat-belt signs were off when the altitude upset occurred, resulting in injuries to passengers and cabin crew.
On landing in Delhi, 20 passengers and four cabin crew members received medical attention.
Twenty people were discharged after treatment for minor injuries, while four people with serious injuries were hospitalised.
The flight crew assessed the situation and decided to continue to Delhi rather than divert to the nearest en-route airport. The aircraft later requested medical priority from Delhi Air Traffic Control and landed safely at IGI Airport at 05:30 UTC.
The incident also caused significant damage inside the cabin, including cracked and deformed ceiling panels, dislocated passenger-service-unit panels, broken handrails and dislodged overhead-bin doors.
The AAIB said its detailed investigation remains in progress. Flight recorders, maintenance and operational records, hydraulic components and samples, as well as other material, are being examined.

briefs.headline: Nearly $750 billion shield: How India built record forex reserves amid the US-Iran war
briefs.deck: How has the RBI managed to secure high forex reserves in times of global economic uncertainty? What’s worked for India and why does the rise in forex cover matter? And, importantly, is it sustainable?
briefs.bodyText:
In May 2026, amid the raging US-Iran war, PM Narendra Modi urged citizens to reduce gold buying, travel abroad and fuel consumption to preserve India’s foreign exchange reserves which had come under pressure due to rupee’s depreciation exacerbated by the Middle East conflict.
Before the start of the war at the end of February, India’s forex reserves had hit a record high, but the 
Reserve Bank of India
’s (RBI) steps to curb rupee’s slide and the drain due to rising fuel costs and gold import values strained the forex reserves.
Now, months after the start of the conflict, India has reported its highest ever foreign exchange reserves of over $740 billion! Forex reserves hit a record high last week itself at $729 billion, and this week has seen a further rise. In fact, reserves have for 9 weeks now!.
How has the RBI managed to secure high forex reserves in times of global economic uncertainty? What’s worked for India and why does the rise in forex cover matter? And, importantly, is it sustainable?
RBI’s FCNR(B) window bonanza
What the RBI did was simple, but with better-than-expected results: The central incentivised Indian banks to attract foreign-currency deposits from overseas Indians. This was done by absorbing the currency-hedging costs on FCNR deposits. 
This helped banks by reducing the exchange-rate risk and allowed them to offer more attractive returns to depositors.
FCNR(B) deposits are essentially foreign-currency deposits that non-resident Indians can hold with Indian banks, with the principal and interest maintained in a foreign currency.
The arrangement also allowed banks to leverage the foreign-currency deposits, with some lenders offering loans several times the original deposit. The initiative helped bring fresh dollar inflows.
What was the FCNR(B) scheme?
And the scheme has resulted in bumper inflows!
RBI has garnered $136.38 billion through the special dollar swap scheme which it launched in June to replenish foreign currency supplies and strengthen its reserves war chest.
The inflows have far exceeded the RBI's initial estimate of about $80 billion. In fact, nearly half the mobilisation came in the final 10 days before the scheme closed on August 31.
FCNR(B) deposits accounted for $127.23 billion, while overseas foreign-currency bonds contributed $5.3 billion and external commercial borrowings $3.9 billion. The programme tapped India's 35-million-strong diaspora and was designed to help support the rupee as it came under pressure.
Forex reserves at record high
Not only that, the structure also allowed NRIs to borrow substantially more than the amount deposited. In some cases, borrowing could be as much as 19 times the deposit, with the borrowed funds placed as FCNR(B) deposits.
This has led to India’s forex reserves touching new records even amid the conflict.
The scheme revived a strategy used during the 2013 taper tantrum, when a similar window attracted about $26 billion and helped fuel a sharp rupee rally. The latest scheme was so successful that RBI ended the FCNR window a month earlier than announced.
What it means for India
Experts attribute a large part of the increase in forex reserves to RBI’s swap window. The added cover works well in the current economic situation, providing an important buffer from external shocks.
Experts also note that while inflows from the swap facility were higher, forex reserves have not seen a commensurate increase due to possible central bank interventions to step rupee’s fall.
“The swap facility has been responsible for the bulk of the recent reserve rebuilding, though the extent of lift is lower than the scale of inflows, implying some offset through intervention and balance-sheet adjustments,” says Radhika Rao, Senior Economist and Executive Director at DBS Bank.
According to Rao, the rise in reserves strengthens India's capacity to manage an oil shock, even if it does not fundamentally alter the economy's dependence on imported energy.
How India mopped up dollars
“FCNR deposits are usually medium-term liabilities and thereby a more durable form of financing. Further out, authorities will be focused on generating more resilient sources, including current-account-generated support, capital inflows, FDI, and remittances to backstop the reserves' stock,” she tells TOI.
Importantly, the increased forex reserves amid global turmoil provide confidence to investors and also keeps the speculators at bay knowing the RBI has the firepower to intervene if there is excessive speculative trade.
Ranen Banerjee, Partner and Leader, Economic Advisory, PwC India says that with forex reserves covering over 10 months of imports, India is in a comfortable position.
“The export margins on refined petroleum products have increased significantly and we are getting some cushion from the exports of these products given the hit on foreign refining capacity. Hence, we have a partial cushion on oil price shocks from these exports,” he explains.
“The FII outflows have ebbed, FDI is improving, investments are growing and given markets have been subdued for almost 2 years, the valuations are normalising. Hence, the forex reserves are unlikely to face any immediate outflow concerns,” he adds.
Madan Sabnavis, Chief Economist, Bank of Baroda is of the view that India’s forex position was strong entering into the crisis, and has now strengthened further.
How India used its diaspora to defend rupee
“Forex reserves were already quite strong covering 10-11 months of imports and hence were resilient. Adding these dollars just makes the position much stronger. At a different level given the rather high forward position of around $100 billion, these incremental deposits would in a way balance them,” he tells TOI.
He adds that the current cushion is durable for at least a year, helping greatly in cushioning the blow. “We have been having a negative balance of payments in the last couple of years. This will make it positive,” he said.
Rupee on upward curve
With record inflows reported, the rupee has appreciated to hit a two-month high. Experts believe that had the window not existed, rupee’s depreciation would have been more rapid.
On Thursday, the rupee strengthened by 49 paise, or 0.5%, to end at 94.48 against the dollar, marking its highest level in two months.
The rupee’s appreciation followed the RBI’s disclosure on Wednesday that its special initiative to attract foreign currency deposits from non-resident Indians had generated several billion dollars of inflows.
DK Srivastava, Chief Policy Advisor at EY India says that in the absence of FCNR contribution, it is likely that the rupee would have depreciated further.
“It may be noted that the pressure on the rupee is driven by market forces, the balance between imports and exports of goods and services, net flow of capital and global crude prices. RBI does not aim to intervene in correcting the direction of change of the exchange rate which is determined by these broader forces. At best, it tries to contain the volatility of the INR/$. This became possible by the FCNR contribution,” he tells TOI.
Rupee vs Dollar: Up upward curve
Caution ahead?
The US-Iran war is far from over and India is still importing energy needs such as crude oil, LPG, and LNG at high prices. Foreign investors are still pulling out money and the global economic headwinds continue.
India’s forex cover has grown, which provides the economy with a credible external sector shield. But, the road ahead may continue to be bumpy in lieu of continued external pressures.
DK Srivastava strikes a cautious stance.
The previous peak of India’s forex reserves was $728.5 billion at the end February 2026 which was almost equal to the $729.3 billion post FCNR scheme, he notes.
“Thus, the present level of forex reserves was already achieved earlier when the balance of trade was more favourable. It is important for India’s forex reserve profile to achieve a more positive balance of trade rather than depend on one time schemes which help to minimize depletion in the forex reserves,” he tells TOI.
Diaspora flows hit $127 billion
Some experts have also flagged the eventual hedging cost for RBI. But reports suggest that the government expects the central bank to face limited material costs from the swap facility.
While economists have estimated that hedging could cost the RBI around 3% of roughly Rs 12 lakh crore, or Rs 36,000 crore, policymakers believe the returns from investing the dollars in US Treasuries could offset these costs.
Even as the reserves touch record high, PM Modi has urged Indians to continue preserving forex. He has asked people not to go for foreign holidays, host weddings abroad, or buy gold unless necessary. And that itself is indicative of the government’s measured approach despite economic resilience.

stories.headline: No special ‘room’ for cricket: IOA draws line on BCCI’s Asian Games stay
stories.deck: The BCCI is considering special housing arrangements for its cricketers during the Asian Games, a choice ultimately dependent on the cricket board's logistical capabilities. Meanwhile, the Indian Olympic Association is committed to equitable treatment for all participants. The available official accommodations are subpar, classified as three-star and four-star, which may not meet player…
stories.bodyText:
New Delhi: If the 
BCCI
 decides its cricketers need to stay outside the official 
Asian Games
 hotels in Aichi-Nagoya, the board will have to take full responsibility for accommodation, food, transport and ensuring that its players reach the venue on time. The Indian Olympic Association (IOA), meanwhile, will not seek separate accommodation arrangements for cricket, as it’s for the cricket body and Organising Committee (OC) to work out an amicable solution.
IOA CEO Raghuram Iyer, speaking to TOI, said the BCCI is free to make its own arrangements if the organisers’ hotels don’t suit its requirements, but the decision and the accompanying logistical responsibility would rest with the Board. The IOA, he stressed, has to ensure equal treatment and the welfare of the entire Indian contingent across 36 sports.
“BCCI CEO Hemang Amin got in touch with us (IOA), and we had a fruitful discussion. They are contemplating sending an advance team to Japan to assess the facilities. The IOA is completely fine with that. Based on their assessment, they can decide whether they want to use the organisers’ facilities or make their own arrangements. 
It is for the BCCI and the organisers to work out the best solution. All sports, athletes, coaches and the entire delegation are treated equally by IOA,” Iyer said.
For now, the Games organisers have a designated accommodation plan for both Indian teams. The men have been allotted the three-star APA Hotel Nagoya Ekimae, while the women have been assigned the four-star Meitetsu Grand Hotel, it’s been learnt. Both properties possess the requisite amenities, though they are a grade below the five-star accommodation to which India’s cricketers are generally accustomed. Rooms will be on a twin-sharing basis, another major bone of contention.
The women, captained by Harmanpreet Kaur, face the first logistical test. They return from the Asia Cup in Dubai on Sept 13 and are scheduled to fly to Nagoya the following day. Their Asian Games campaign begins directly in the quarterfinals on Sept 18, with their tournament scheduled to conclude on Sept 22.
The men, led by 
Shreyas Iyer
, will travel later, leaving for Japan on Sept 21. They too enter directly at the quarterfinal stage, with their campaign running from Sept 28 and the team scheduled to return on Oct 4.
With both teams having different arrival windows, the BCCI is now looking at the accommodation and logistics from its own perspective. An advance team is travelling to Japan early next week to inspect the hotels, cricket venue and other facilities before the Board takes a final call, sources revealed.
The availability of suitable alternatives could be crucial. Aichi-Nagoya is already under considerable accommodation pressure, with the number of athletes and coaches expected to rise to around 17,000 from an original planning figure of 15,000. Existing hotels are being supplemented by mobile accommodation and the Costa Serena cruise ship.
If the BCCI decides the official hotels do not work for its teams and opts for separate properties, it will have to arrange the entire operation, including rooms, food, local transport and travel to and from the cricket venue, while ensuring the players reach the ground well ahead of match time.
That arrangement, however, would not put the cricketers outside the Games system. The BCCI would have to communicate its decision through the IOA to the organisers, and all Games-related security, accreditation and access protocols would continue to apply. Outsiders without valid accreditation would not be permitted into the team hotels.
The separate stay would also have implications for anti-doping procedures. WADA and International Testing Agency (ITA) dope-control officers would have to be informed of the players’ location so that random testing can be carried out at their chosen accommodation.
Iyer said the IOA was comfortable with the BCCI assessing what works best for its players.
“The BCCI is taking care of its athletes, and sending an advance team is the right way to assess the facilities before making a decision. We are completely for the well-being of the athletes. Our objective is that the entire Indian delegation has a comfortable stay and a wonderful experience in Japan,” he said.
The contrast with Los Angeles 2028 is already emerging
While Japan’s cricket arrangements have prompted scrutiny, planning for cricket’s Olympic return at Los Angeles 2028 is already well advanced. Iyer was part of a joint IOA-Sports Authority of India (SAI) delegation that recently spent nearly a week in Los Angeles, meeting stakeholders and inspecting facilities across sports, including cricket.
“The objective is to ensure athletes can focus only on their performance and do not face logistical issues. We are thinking well in advance about their welfare, comfort and acclimatisation, and this is something which is happening for the first time,” Iyer said.
Cricket’s LA28 venue, the newly built Knight Riders Cricket Ground at the Fairplex complex in Pomona, is located next to the Sheraton Fairplex Suites & Conference Center, where the cricket teams are expected to be accommodated. Major League Cricket matches are also expected to provide an early competitive test of the new venue and playing surface.
Before the Asian Games, India and Japan will also share a historic cricketing moment. Their men’s teams meet in a T20I on Sept 22 for the Suzuki Cup, marking 75 years of diplomatic relations and giving India valuable match practice ahead of the Games.

stories.headline: Mature Gurindervir battles stopwatch, questions, injuries
stories.deck: India’s fastest man has endured a challenging few months since breaching the 10.1-second barrier. Ahead of the Asian Games, he is determined to take control of his life and his running
stories.bodyText:
Two years ago, Gurindervir Singh stamped his return to the top rung of sprinters in India by winning the National Inter-State Athletics Championships in the fading light at Panchkula.
It was only 10.32 seconds, but it brought him the spotlight and support needed to kick his almost stagnant career back into gear. In time, it led to him becoming the fastest Indian on the track, raising expectations of a historic sub-10 run in the most glamorous event in athletics.
Familiar situation
As the 25-year-old prepares for the upcoming Asian Games, the parallels between 2024 and now are hard to miss, even for the man himself.
Back then, Gurindervir was the meet record holder at the Nationals, but, in the three years since he had clocked 10.27s (Patiala, 2021), others had raced far ahead. Coupled with injuries, lack of sufficient nutrition and uncertainty over his sporting future, he had been forced to play catch-up.
Now, with the all-important continental meet looming large, Gurindervir is again battling the stopwatch on the track and questions and injuries off it.
The only Indian to go under 10.1s has had a torrid few months ever since the incredible two days in May when the national record switched hands thrice, Gurindervir eventually making it his own in 10.09s. He injured his hamstring, crashed out in the first round at the Commonwealth Games and finished a lowly seventh at the World Athletics Continental Tour in Bhubaneswar.
The big difference now, however, is the support he has access to. Picked up by the Reliance Foundation after the 2024 outing and working under the watchful eyes of its athletics director James Hillier at the high performance centre in Navi Mumbai, Gurindervir is already back to peak training ahead of his biggest outing of the year.
“He’s had a good couple of weeks of training. He’s getting back into good shape but he’s looking to get into peak 100m shape within the next two weeks. That’s what I’m hoping for,” Hillier said before getting into the details of Gurindervir’s technical strengths and weaknesses.
“CWG … there were certain elements of his race that were quite good from a coaching perspective. I’m very happy with the first 60-70 meters of his race. What we’ve been working on in the last few weeks is getting him to extrapolate that speed over the full 100m.
“We’ve been working pretty hard to get that last bit of the race sorted. I’ve put some specific training in place for that. We have a competition in Delhi on September 10 and that’s going to be a key competition. We’ll get to see exactly where he is, where the training is going and how well he finishes the race there, that’ll give us very good information,” Hillier explained.
The transformation
The man himself has gone from being an emotional and often-stressed youngster to a more confident and mature professional who is determined to take control of his life and his running, something Hillier also acknowledged. The transformation began in March last year, when he broke the national record for the first time with a 10.20s run at the Indian Grand Prix 1.
Gurindervir had been battling stomach ulcers that weakened his body and naysayers who tried to break his spirit. Both were spillovers from his time in obscurity before 2024 — when a poor diet and dirty water stripped away his gut lining. He could barely keep anything in and lost almost 15kgs in a fortnight even as people, known and unknown, sniggered that he was finished.
“If you had asked last year’s Gurindervir about handling the pressure, maybe he would have been in stress. That time too, all this happened with me — interviews, phone calls, questions, expectations. I was not sleeping at night,” he said.
“Back then, I couldn’t get out of it. I was thinking about what to say in the next interview when I should have been thinking about how to improve. When I ran in the Fed Cup [in 2025], I cramped and it stressed me even more because I had claimed I would do a lot in the interviews. That Gurindervir took pressure. This one has evolved, he has learnt from all this.”
A large part of the credit for that, he insisted, went to Hillier for keeping him away from a lot of negativity. “If it wasn’t for him, I would have been in a very bad, stressful situation. The coach motivated me a lot. He gave me the right guidance on how to deal with it.”
A lot of people had been critical of his inclusion for Glasgow, questioning his fitness, but Hillier has already clarified that the problem was not carrying an injury into competition but the lack of sufficient races before the CWG because of the injury. That issue has been addressed although the Continental Tour event highlighted the issues that continue to plague his race plan.
“At the Bhubaneswar event, you’ll see he was in a really good position at 60-70m and then sort of fell away, which I expected to happen based on what’s been happening in training. It’s just how he’s put together,” Hillier said.
“Many 100m athletes run the race in different ways. Guri is a very good accelerator and that’s just his natural strength. He won the national indoor 60m earlier in the year, broke the national record in that with a very fast time of 6.60s. Someone like an Animesh [Kujur] or an Amlan [Borgohain], these guys tend to finish strong, that’s their natural strength. We must train them to their strengths and then work alongside that to manage their weaknesses.”
Listening to his body
Gurindervir has also learnt to listen to his body. “I have worked on everything. What I eat and how much, how much I travel. If I am feeling any pain, how much effort do I have to put into the workout? If I am doing an endurance workout, how do I do it?
“In weight training, I have set levels I must achieve every month. It’s the same on track as well. I will train as much as my body needs. I discuss with the dietician how much food I need. I had some lack of mobility before, so sitting with the physio, knowing which muscles and joints I have to work on so that I can run better.”
The one thing that hasn’t changed, however, is Gurindervir’s conviction. The reason he was stressed, he explained, was because what he says matters to him.
“If I say something, it has to have meaning. Words are important for me. If I claim or promise something and I cannot do it, it affects me. That’s my nature. My father had a dream, I started running to fulfil that dream. People said Indians can’t be competitive in 100m, I was determined to do it. It will take some time, but it will definitely happen.”

stories.headline: I have a choice to live with gratitude or anger; I choose gratitude: Shannon Rowbury
stories.deck: The former middle-distance runner will have waited 16 years by the time she receives her Olympic bronze at LA28. She talks about competing in an era when many of her competitors were doping, her emotions when she heard she would finally get justice, her passion to advocate for clean sport and the switch from athlete to commentator
stories.bodyText:
Born about a month after the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics, former American middle-distance runner Shannon Rowbury is eagerly awaiting her women’s 1500m bronze medal at LA28. She richly deserved a podium finish 14 years ago, but was robbed of the honour due to the drug-induced performances of some competitors. Thanks to the International Olympic Committee’s (IOC) ceaseless war against doping, the tainted athletes, who finished ahead of her, have been disqualified, and Rowbury stands to formally receive her medal more than a decade-and-a-half after winning it.
As part of an Athletics Federation of India (AFI) initiative, Rowbury, now a commentator who also actively participates in anti-doping drives, was in India to train the country’s athletics commentators and work during the World Athletics Continental Tour Silver meet at the Kalinga Stadium in Bhubaneswar last month. She shared her compelling story, full of mixed emotions. Excerpts:
How was your first visit to India?
I was so excited for my first trip to India to be for such a meaningful event — to be part of the Indian meet, to do the in-stadium commentary, and to work with aspiring Indian broadcasters. It has been a really magical first visit. Hopefully not my last.
Could you tell us how you shifted from athletics to broadcasting?
I started while I was still competing. I stopped competing in 2021, but I had started broadcasting in 2017 for smaller meets, mostly distance events where I had experience. I could provide analysis and colour commentary, with insight into what might be going through the athlete’s head and the tactics. Over the years my roles have grown. I get tingles when I smell the track and hear the sounds. It has helped me stay connected to the sport.
There is always a gap between the broadcaster/media and the athletes. Do you think misunderstanding creates a gap?
My experience as an athlete helps me be a better broadcaster, not just because I understand what it’s like to be in those races, but because I have compassion. Our athletes work for 365 days, but they only get maybe 15 or 20 opportunities to race. It’s hard to maintain a high level year after year. When I cover a race, I try to share the effort and the meaning within the season, and to understand that these are humans who seem like superheroes.
How do you look back at your career?
I’m most proud of my longevity. I spent a decade ranked in the top ten in the world, which is not an easy feat. Unfortunately, during much of my career, many athletes who were ultimately caught for doping were competing. The story of my Olympic medal is still ongoing. I will receive it physically at the LA Olympics in 2028. It was heartbreaking to compete in a time that wasn’t as clean or fair as it should have been, but it gives me passion to fight for fair sport and excitement to cheer for athletes in races that feel level.
Could you elaborate on your wait for the medal?
In London 2012, I finished sixth but in the 12-13 years since, five women from my race have been disqualified, including the gold and silver medallists [Asli Cakir Alptekin and Gamze Bulut] from Turkey and a Russian athlete [Tatyana Tomashova], who was ahead of me and was disqualified just last year. That officially moved me into bronze. The IOC’s policy now is to offer medal ceremonies, so I will have a ceremony in LA. It’s nothing like London, but I’m grateful to have the opportunity to celebrate in front of friends and family. I’m grateful to a system that committed itself to clean sport.
It will be 16 years by the time I get it. When I found out, my entire body started shaking. I started sobbing. I had carried so much frustration about the unfairness. But I am an optimistic person...I got justice and I will receive my medal in front of my two children. They’ll see their mother being recognised for winning with integrity, winning the right way. Hopefully that will reinforce lessons, not only for them but for others, that truth can triumph. If I could change the past, I would make that race fair. Since I cannot, I channel those hard moments into advocacy, change and hopefully inspiration. I have a choice to live with gratitude or anger, and I choose gratitude.
At the Olympics, my highest finish after London was fourth in Rio, so it was very challenging to know London had a lot of cheats. I had a medal at the World Championships, but an Olympic medal is on another level.
How has the middle-distance field changed in the last few years?
There has been a lot of innovation around shoe technology, kind of fuelling the way athletes train, the lifting and recovery they do. Those developments have created a new wave of world records and personal bests. In the United States we call it trackflation — times across the board are so much quicker. It’s exciting because it creates new stories and exciting moments when a record is broken and an athlete improves. It’s a good sign...because it means our sport is growing.
You spoke about doping. India is among the countries with the most doping-related violations. How should the AFI approach this?
Part of it for me was how I was raised — it wasn’t just about winning, it was about sportsmanship and how you win. It’s important to create an ecosystem that incentivises performance but prioritises fairness, and enforces penalties for those who cheat. Once there is a clear directive that cheats will lose eligibility, that will disincentivise it.
India has high-achieving athletes and international figures. There’s so much more that can be done to develop younger talent and build strong foundations so they have a career not just as professional athletes but also as coaches, broadcasters or in other roles beyond their athletics career.
Since you have been affected by doping, do you do anything on education?
I work with the US Anti-Doping Agency (USADA) to share my story. I’ve attended conferences. It has been about explaining the human side of doping. At events about education around drug testing, I meet people working to improve testing technology and give them a sense of who they are doing it for. There’s a large group committed to clean sport, and I get to thank them in person and help them understand how impactful their work is.
LA is two years away, and the World Championships is next year. How do you look forward to the middle-distance events?
The depth, especially in the 1500m on both men’s and women’s sides, is astonishing. It makes for great racing when more than half the field in an Olympic or World final could potentially be on the podium. I love a close, exciting race, because it makes for drama.

stories.headline: Footballer quits after being sold to rival club for 15kg of pork sausage
stories.deck: In 2006, Romanian defender Marius Cioara moved from UT Arad to Regal Hornia for an unusual transfer fee: 15kg of pork sausages. Constant teasing over the deal reportedly drove him to retire the next day. He later moved to Spain to work on a farm. Similarly, Norwegian footballer Kenneth Kristiansen was transferred for 75kg of shrimp, matching his body weight.
stories.bodyText:
Transfer fees in football have reached eye-watering levels, with clubs happily throwing around millions for the right player. But back in 2006, one Romanian defender discovered that a transfer could also be settled in a rather more… edible fashion.
Marius Cioara was playing for fourth-tier UT Arad when he moved to second-division Regal Hornia. The fee was not money, though. It was 15 kilograms of pork sausages.
UT Arad, officially known as Asociația Fotbal Club UTA Arad, is one of Romania’s historic clubs. Founded in 1945, the Arad side, nicknamed Bătrâna Doamnă, or “The Old Lady,” has won six national titles and two Romanian Cups. These days, UTA play in Romania’s top flight, the SuperLiga, in their red and white colours at the Francisc von Neuman Stadium.
But in 2006, the club’s transfer dealings were apparently a little less glamorous.
And somehow, that was only the beginning of the story.
A transfer fee with a very short shelf life
Cioara's unusual move quickly became a source of jokes at his new club, and according to comments attributed to the defender by local media, the teasing eventually became too much.
"The sausage taunts all got too much," Cioara said.
He added: "They were joking, but I would have got more from the Germans and making sausage jokes was a huge insult."
The defender decided he had had enough and retired from football the very next day.
Cioara subsequently left the game altogether and moved to Spain, where he found work on a farm. Whether the change of scenery finally gave him some peace from the sausage jokes is unfortunately not documented, but at least nobody could accuse him of taking the whole thing too seriously.
Regal Hornia, meanwhile, apparently wanted its unusual transfer fee back. The club asked UT Arad to return the 15kg of sausages, giving the story perhaps its most bizarre post-transfer twist.
He wasn't even the only player transferred for food
As strange as Cioara's deal sounds, he was not the only footballer whose transfer was settled with something from the kitchen.
During the 2000-01 season, Norwegian third-tier player Kenneth Kristiansen moved from Vindbjart to Flekkeroy in a deal where the fee was calculated according to his weight.
The currency? Shrimp.
Kristiansen weighed 75kg, so Flekkeroy effectively paid 75kg of shrimp for him.
Flekkeroy chairman Rolf Guttormsen recalled being unsure whether the deal was actually serious.
"I had no idea if it was a joke or deadly serious," he said. "The Vindbjart chairman said that it was a bit of both, but they wanted the shrimp."
Fortunately, there was no shortage of seafood.
"No problem, we have enough shrimp," Guttormsen added.
So while modern football has given us nine-figure transfers, release clauses and add-ons that require a calculator, there was a time when clubs could apparently settle their transfer business with a trip to the butcher or fish market.
Cioara got 15kg of sausages. Kristiansen got his shrimp deal.
And, presumably, somewhere in Italy, a sporting director is still wondering what the going rate for a decent midfielder is in frozen pizzas.

briefs.headline: One fight left on UFC deal, but Page knows his title route: ‘It's middleweight’
briefs.deck: Michael ‘Venom’ Page wants to restart the momentum he feels has slowed during his UFC run. After moving between welterweight and middleweight, the 39-year-old now sees 185 pounds as his route towards the title. His next test is No. 15 Nursulton Ruziboev, a dangerous submission fighter. With one fight left on his UFC contract, Page wants a performance that can lead to bigger fights and a new deal.
briefs.bodyText:
Two-and-a-half years into his UFC career, Michael ‘Venom’ Page is down to the last fight of his original six-fight deal. The 39-year-old has won four of five, fought at two weight classes and is now back at middleweight, where he says he sees his route to a UFC title.
For all the changes, Page feels his UFC run has not built the momentum he expected. The loss to Ian Machado Garry at welterweight was followed by wins over Shara Magomedov and former middleweight title challenger Jared Cannonier, but his return to 170 pounds for Sam Patterson did not lead to the run of fights he had hoped for.
“I feel like I had momentum, and it slowed down,” Page told 
TimesofIndia.com
 ahead of his middleweight fight against Nursulton Ruziboev at UFC Fight Night in Paris. “So this fight is to restart that momentum again, and build towards the top.”
Page looks to restart his momentum at 185
Page's move between the divisions has been tied to that search for momentum. After his wins at middleweight, he wanted to return to welterweight because he saw fights there that interested him. But, he said, getting opponents to agree to those fights became difficult.
“I wanted to go back to welterweight, just because I feel like there’s some really exciting fights at welterweight,” Page said. 
“But the guys at welterweight don't like to fight regularly enough for me, and I wasn't getting enough people saying yes to wanting to fight me, so it made more sense to go to middleweight, because I feel like I'll have regular fights.”
That brought him back to 185 pounds, where Page now says the title route is clear.
“Well, I've solidified myself now at middleweight, so it's gonna be middleweight,” he said when asked which division he sees himself fighting for a UFC title in.
The move up has also suited him physically. Page said he feels stronger at middleweight without losing the speed that has been one of the defining parts of his game.
“They gave me more food,” Page said with a chuckle. “To eat more, and feel a lot stronger. So yeah, I definitely feel stronger. I equally still feel as fast, but I feel a lot faster than the guys at middleweight, just because I'm used to exploding and keeping up with welterweights. So the middleweights, I feel my speed is even better there.”
Ruziboev brings a different test for Page
The next step is Ruziboev, who is ranked No. 15 at middleweight and comes into Paris on a three-fight UFC winning streak. The Uzbek is 5-0 in the division, with his only UFC defeat coming in his lone appearance at welterweight.
His most recent win was another reminder of the danger he carries on the ground. Ruziboev submitted Andrey Pulyaev in the first round in June, taking his career total to 21 submission wins, according to his UFC record.
Page is not expecting to be able to switch off that part of the fight.
“Yeah, I think he's a long, rangy fighter. And as you say, he's got very good submissions, so that's definitely his dangerous area,” Page said. “So yeah, it's making sure I don't get caught up in anything where he can use that advantage against me. If we're on the ground, it's because I've gone for the takedown, or I've taken him down, and not the other way around. Can't let him take my back, you know, I have to just be vigilant in the grappling area, and then do exactly what I do well in the striking area.”
Ruziboev's run at middleweight has been one of the more consistent parts of his UFC career. After his brief move to welterweight, he returned to 185 pounds and has won three straight, including the Pulyaev submission.
One fight left, and a title route in mind
For Page, though, the opponent is only part of what makes Saturday important. It is his last fight on the current UFC contract, and he has been open about wanting a new deal - provided it gives him a clearer route towards the bigger fights and, eventually, the title.
He has previously described the difficulty of getting a Top-10 opponent as frustrating, saying he had been looking for bigger names over his previous three fights. But Page does not want the contract situation to bleed into fight night.
“Yeah, like I said, just having interviews and speaking about it is just what it is. I don't… after the interview's finished, I don't think about it,” he said. “The only thought is Saturday, making sure my fight's good, and making sure I feel the best, and I go out there and just put on a performance.”
That performance could also answer a question that has followed the Bellator standout through his UFC run. He arrived in the promotion known for spectacular finishes, but all five of his UFC fights so far have gone to the judges. His last three - against Cannonier, Patterson and Ruziboev - have come after the move into the middleweight picture.
At 39, Page knows the window is not getting wider. What he wants now is a run that moves quickly enough to matter. For the next six months, at least, there will be plenty happening outside the cage too. Page said he has acting work and auditions alongside his training.
“It looks… it looks very, very busy, because I'm not only gonna be fighting, but I'm doing some acting stuff as well, so it's gonna be very, very busy, but it still looks like a lot of training, and… and now a lot of auditions.”

briefs.headline: KCL | Anand’s late-game heroics put Titans in final
briefs.deck: Globstars stun Ripples in the second semifinal
briefs.bodyText:
Tailender Anand Joseph turned out to be the unlikely hero as his breathtaking three-ball unbeaten 16 pulled off a heist for Thrissur Titans at the Sports Hub Greenfield stadium here on Thursday. His heroics punched Titans’ ticket for the Kerala Cricket League final with a one-wicket win over Trivandrum Royals.
Titans needed 15 from the last over bowled by Rahul Chandran and the left-arm pacer piled on the pressure by conceding only two runs from the first two deliveries. However, Anand launched the third ball over long-off for a towering six, slammed the next one past mid-on for a four and sealed the win with a six over mid-wicket.
Earlier, Anand snuffed out the dangerous Vishnu Vinod and in-form captain Krishna Prasad to reduce Royals to 31 for two.
Left-arm spinner Biju Narayan’s tidy spell of two for 20 saw Royals slump to 93 for five. However, Akshay Manohar (53 n.o., 26b, 4x4, 3x6) and M. Nikhil (28 n.o., 15b, 2x4, 2x6) added 70 from 35 balls for the sixth wicket to raise the total to 163 for five. Titans lost its openers early but a 45-run third-wicket stand between Ahammed Imran (43) and Shoun Roger (23) put the chase back on track. Captain S. Akhil (27) kept his team in the hunt even as wickets fell regularly in the death overs. It looked like curtains for Titans when Akhil perished in the 19th over but Anand’s sensational knock took them home.
Calicut Globstars crushed Alleppey Ripples by 36 runs and will meet Titans in the final on Saturday.
After piling up 218 for five, thanks to half-centuries from Varun Nayanar (59) and Abdul Basith (53), Globstars restricted Ripples to 182 for eight.
Ripples’ chase fizzled out after Jose Perayil ended the threatening 152-run third-wicket stand between Sachin Baby (72) and K.A. Arun (82).
The scores: Trivandrum Royals 163/5 in 20 overs (Akshay Manohar 53 n.o., Biju Narayanan 2/20, Anand Joseph 2/31) lost to Thrissur Titans 167/9 in 19.5 overs (Ahammed Imran 42, Rahul Chandran 3/32, M. Nikhil 2/29).
Calicut Globstars 218/5 in 20 overs (Varun Nayanar 59. Rohan Kunnummal 45, Abdul Basith 53, Ajith Raj 2/27) bt Alleppey Ripples 182/8 in 20 overs (Sachin Baby 73, K.A. Arun 82, Jose Perayil 3/33, Ibnul Afthab 2/20, Akhil Scaria 2/39).

briefs.headline: Women's Asia Cup: India favourites against arch-foes Pakistan
briefs.deck: Ahead of the game, both India openers Smriti Mandhana and Shafali Verma looked at the top of their game.
briefs.bodyText:
Having already made the semifinals, a far superior India will be expected to step up the intensity against traditional foe Pakistan in their final league game of the Women's Asia Cup on Saturday (September 5, 2026).
Men or women, routinely scheduled Indo-Pak fixtures in multi-team events have not lived up to the off-field hype for a while now.
Nothing different is expected when the two teams meet at the Dubai International Stadium, with overwhelming title favourites India expected to steamroll Pakistan.
That is not to say that India don't have work to do in the shortest format, having made premature exits in the past two World Cups.
They need to develop a pool of power-hitters and fast bowlers to challenge the hegemony of Australia.
However, at the Asia level, no side comes close to India's level. The Indians had somehow finished runners-up to Sri Lanka in the previous edition. Pakistan, on the other hand, have won their opening game against Thailand and remain in contention for the last-four stage.
Ahead of the game, both India openers Smriti Mandhana and Shafali Verma looked at the top of their game. Mandhana broke a battery of records against Hong Kong en route a memorable hundred to fire out a warning for the other teams in the competition.
The pitches here have not been the easiest to bat on.
The batters usually take about 10 balls or so to assess the pace of the surface and accordingly plan their innings. This is exactly what both Mandhana and Shafali did on Thursday night.
The likes of Pratika Rawal, Richa Ghosh and skipper Harmanpreet Kaur will look to spend more time in the middle, having not been able to convert starts.
Pressure is mounting on new number three Rawal, who has not been able to meet the demands of the T20 game, having found plenty of success in the ODI format.
The addition of Nandani Sharma in the pace attack is a step in the right direction as she is delivering on her promise while opening the bowling alongside spearhead Kranti Gaud.
Pakistan, on the other hand, need drastic improvement in their batting to competing with India. The shortcomings in the batting department have let the team down for a number of years.
Even in their last game against Thailand, Pakistan found themselves under pressure in the powerplay with the loss of three wickets. However, they managed to defend a lowly 119 against a less-established side.
The team over-relies on opener Muneeba Ali and bowling all-rounder Fatima Sana who is also the captain of the side. That will need to change if Pakistan are to challenge their mighty rivals.

briefs.headline: Piers Morgan calls Messi’s GOAT ad the ‘most arrogant’ and ‘shameless’ bragging ever
briefs.deck: Lionel Messi’s latest Michelob Ultra advert declares him the GOAT, but Piers Morgan strongly disagrees. The outspoken Cristiano Ronaldo supporter called the campaign “the most arrogant” bragging in sports and used Messi’s international retirement to argue Ronaldo’s superior 146-goal record settles the debate. Despite their rivalry, Ronaldo recently sent Messi a supportive message following his…
briefs.bodyText:
Lionel Messi
 may have just retired from international football, but apparently the Messi-Ronaldo GOAT debate did not get the memo.
The Argentina legend has been at the centre of the argument for years, and his latest appearance in a Michelob Ultra advertising campaign has given 
Piers Morgan
 another reason to make his own feelings known. The advert turns Messi's remarkable international career into a giant bar receipt, ticking off his goals, assists, minutes and major trophies before ending with a rather cheeky verdict: "GOAT debate-settled."
Morgan, a long-time 
Cristiano Ronaldo
 supporter, was not particularly impressed.
Messi's career becomes a bar tab
The Michelob Ultra campaign shared on Messi's Instagram takes a playful approach to his Argentina career, presenting his achievements as though they have been added to a restaurant or bar receipt.
Instead of simply listing his honours, the advert runs through the numbers and milestones that helped define his time in the famous blue and white shirt. His goals, assists and minutes are all included, while the list also highlights his biggest international achievements, including the 2022 FIFA World Cup, multiple Copa América titles, Olympic gold and the Finalissima.
It even nods to the millions of fans Messi has inspired throughout his career before arriving at that final line: "GOAT debate-settled."
Importantly, that was the advertising campaign's conclusion rather than Messi personally declaring himself the greatest player ever.
That distinction did not stop Morgan from having his say.
The British journalist, who has repeatedly backed Ronaldo in the long-running debate, described the campaign as "the most arrogant piece of shameless bragging in the history of sport" and called it "Hilarious" in a post on social media.
It was a typically strong reaction even from someone who has made no secret of where he stands.
Morgan used Messi's retirement to make the Ronaldo case
Morgan's latest comments came just days after Messi announced his retirement from international football, bringing the curtain down on a 21-year Argentina career.
The 39-year-old leaves with 207 appearances and 125 goals, making him Argentina's record appearance-maker and leading goalscorer. His international career ultimately delivered the major prizes that had once seemed to elude him, including the World Cup and Copa América.
His retirement followed a difficult few weeks. Argentina lost to Spain in the 2026 World Cup final, Messi's second defeat in a World Cup final after the 2014 loss to Germany, while his father, Jorge Messi, died at the age of 68 just weeks later.
Ronaldo also reached out to Messi following the death of his father, offering a more personal message amid the difficult period.
Commenting on Instagram, the Portugal captain wrote: "A huge hug to you and your loved ones during these difficult times, Leo. Stay strong."
The message offered a reminder that, despite the fierce comparisons between the pair and the constant debate among their supporters, Ronaldo and Messi have maintained mutual respect throughout their careers.
Morgan responded to the retirement announcement on August 31 by immediately turning the conversation towards Ronaldo.
"Breaking: Lionel Messi retires from international football, after scoring 125 goals for the Argentina national team, placing him second on the list of highest international goalscorers," Morgan wrote.
He then followed it with the comparison he clearly wanted to make.
"Cristiano Ronaldo has scored 146 goals for the Portugal national team, the highest figure in the history of football at international level. This settles the debate over who is the best player in history," he added.
Morgan has previously left Messi out of his all-time XI despite the Argentine's eight Ballon d'Or wins and extraordinary collection of team honours. He has also named four players he considers better than Messi.
His position is hardly surprising given his long-standing friendship with Ronaldo, and the two superstars have spent much of their careers being compared with one another.
Even with Messi now stepping away from international football, it seems that particular argument is going nowhere. If anything, it has found a new receipt.

briefs.headline: ‘Someone is smoking weed’: Sabalenka stops US Open match mid-game — Watch
briefs.deck: In an unexpected turn during her US Open match, world number one Aryna Sabalenka was distracted by a strong cannabis odor. Noticing the smell while facing Kamilla Rakhimova, she promptly alerted the chair umpire, leading to a consultation with tournament officials. This peculiar incident is reportedly linked to park regulations in the area. Despite the unusual challenge, Sabalenka maintained her…
briefs.bodyText:
World No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka encountered an unusual distraction during her US Open third-round match on Friday when a strong cannabis smell reached the court at Louis Armstrong Stadium.
Sabalenka was facing Uzbekistan’s Kamilla Rakhimova and had made a fast start, leading 3-0 when she briefly stopped play during her second service game. She approached chair umpire Eva Asderaki-Moore and pointed out the strong odour.
Sabalenka alerts umpire during match
Sabalenka told the umpire: "Someone is smoking weed. Would you mind to... because it's so strong."
Asderaki-Moore immediately contacted tournament officials over the complaint and made a smoking gesture to alert staff. Members of the US Open team then moved into the stands to try to locate the source of the smell.
The interruption was brief and Sabalenka quickly returned her attention to the match. She maintained control against Rakhimova and eventually secured a 6-3, 6-4 victory to advance to the fourth round.
Cannabis smell becomes recurring US Open issue
The incident highlighted an issue that has surfaced repeatedly at this year's tournament. The Billie Jean King National Tennis Center sits next to Flushing Meadows-Corona Park, where recreational cannabis use is legal for adults aged 21 and over in New York.
However, smoking of any kind is prohibited inside the US Open grounds, meaning the smell drifting over from the surrounding park has become an unwelcome distraction for some players. British player Katie Boulter had previously spoken about noticing the smell around the venue, particularly near Court 17.
"I have experienced it," Boulter said. "You got down to the practice courts and down in the park courts, you do smell it a lot."
"I’m not a huge fan of it. I know a lot of players have complained on specific courts. I’ve played on (Court 17) before and I did smell it during my match. It’s something that I wouldn’t like to smell in the middle of my match."
In response, the USTA shared the following statement: 'While we can’t control what takes place off the grounds of the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, we continue to be vigilant as we maintain this facility as a smoke-free environment.
Sabalenka keeps title defence on track
Despite the unexpected interruption, Sabalenka stayed composed and closed out another straight-sets victory. The world No. 1, who is defending her US Open title, therefore advanced without dropping a set against Rakhimova and continued her bid for another championship in New York.

briefs.headline: ‘This is a mistake’: Srikkanth slams India’s ‘fear-driven’ squad for Afghanistan series
briefs.deck: Former cricketer Kris Srikkanth criticised India's squad selection for the Afghanistan series. He believes selectors missed an opportunity to test younger players. Srikkanth described the decision as a mistake influenced by recent defeats. The selectors opted for an experienced team instead of experimenting with new talent. This approach was seen as a safe move after losses in Ireland and England.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: India’s decision to field a full-strength squad for the upcoming Afghanistan T20I series has drawn sharp criticism from former cricketer 
Kris Srikkanth
, who believes the selectors missed a valuable opportunity to expose more youngsters to international cricket.
Srikkanth described the selection as a “mistake” and suggested that the recent defeats in Ireland and England had influenced the selectors into playing it safe rather than experimenting with the squad.
India suffered a 0-2 T20I series defeat against Ireland before being beaten 0-4 by England in July. With the Afghanistan series offering three matches in familiar home conditions, Srikkanth felt it was the ideal setting to give fringe players a longer run.
“After the series losses in Ireland and England, the selectors have decided not to take a chance and picked a full-strength squad for Afghanistan. They are going all guns blazing, but this is a mistake. It's against teams like Afghanistan that you should try out youngsters. Instead, you've picked a full-strength squad out of fear,” Srikkanth said on his YouTube channel.
‘A desperation move’ after England, Ireland losses
Srikkanth also questioned why the selectors had moved so quickly back towards an experienced combination after using the Zimbabwe series to test players outside the regular setup.
“It feels like a desperation move after the Ireland and England losses. But this squad is almost the same as the one they picked for England,” he added.
India have named a 15-member squad for the three T20Is, with Shreyas Iyer continuing as captain and Tilak Varma as his deputy. Jasprit Bumrah, Sanju Samson, Ishan Kishan, Axar Patel, Arshdeep Singh, Shivam Dube and Varun Chakaravarthy are among the experienced names included, while 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has retained his place after an encouraging Zimbabwe series.
The Afghanistan series will be played in New Delhi on September 13, 15 and 17, with all three games scheduled at the Arun Jaitley Stadium.
Bumrah's return is, however, subject to fitness clearance, as are Nitish Kumar Reddy, Washington Sundar and Harshit Rana. Hardik Pandya, meanwhile, has missed out after suffering another setback during his rehabilitation.
Srikkanth questions ‘match fitness’
The former India captain also raised concerns over the inclusion of players whose match fitness remains untested.
“These four have not proved match-fitness. So on what basis are they subject to fitness? Just because you prove your fitness at the Bengaluru CoE, are you fit? That's how Harshit Rana went to England, and then what happened to him there? So match fitness is important,” said Srikkanth.
His comments come as Bumrah, Nitish, Sundar and Rana are all awaiting fitness clearance before their participation in the Afghanistan series is confirmed.
For Srikkanth, however, the bigger issue is the opportunity cost. Rather than using the three-match series to assess emerging options, he believes India have responded to their recent setbacks by reverting to a familiar combination.

briefs.headline: SAI creates ‘Little Japan’ in India: Athletes get a taste of Asian Games life in containers
briefs.deck: The Sports Authority of India has launched a unique facility inspired by Japanese culture, featuring accommodations fashioned from shipping containers. These two-bedroom units are equipped with contemporary amenities, immersing athletes in Japanese cuisine such as ramen, sushi, and tempura crafted by skilled chefs. This endeavour is geared towards helping athletes adjust to Japan ahead of the…
briefs.bodyText:
BENGALURU: Shipping containers with exteriors painted with cherry blossoms and chochins — traditional Japanese lanterns -- hung on the sides have been transformed into two-bedroom accommodation. Inside are modern amenities, an LED screen displaying information about the Asian Games and Japanese books such as Ikigai and Kaizen. The menu features ramen, an assortment of sushi, tempura and yakitori.
This could easily be Japan. It isn’t, yet.
It is the Sports Authority of India (SAI) South Centre in Bengaluru.
To help Asian Games-bound athletes acclimatise to the culture, living conditions, and food they will encounter in Japan, SAI has created a slice of the country at its South Centre and the facility in Patiala. Athletes from several disciplines have already utilised the facilities, with team-sport athletes expected to be accommodated in the containers.
The containers, built at a cost of around Rs 20 lakh, resulted from an idea conceived earlier this year.
“We planned to do this in January, but due to various factors, we could not get them ready. The containers have been operational for a week now, and the volleyball team were one of the first to experience it,” Vishnu Sudhakaran, regional director of the SAI South Centre, told TOI.
Each container can accommodate four athletes and was completed in 45 days. Besides overnight stays, the facility has also been used during the day by track and field athletes and the women’s hockey team.
And this is not a temporary arrangement. The structure has been designed for permanent use.
“Our athletes spend a lot of time away from home and often more than two family members visit them for short durations. We will use this facility as a transit accommodation for visiting families of athletes,” Sudhakaran said.
TASTE OF JAPAN
The effort to recreate a Japanese experience has extended to the cafeteria.
While continental food was introduced last year to help athletes travelling to Europe acclimatise to the cuisine, Japanese dishes were gradually added to the menu from January this year.
Chefs at the SAI Centre underwent specialised training in Japanese cuisine under chef Vaibhav Soni of Snowy Foods.
“First, the athletes and the chefs were introduced to Japanese culture, such as what and why they eat a particular kind of food, the ingredients they use and what they prefer during breakfast, lunch and dinner,” Soni explained.
“The chefs were then taken through the theoretical process followed by the practical knowledge of it. They were then trained in the preparation of various kinds of ramen, sushi, robatayaki, tempura, etc,” he added.
Soni has been making regular visits to the centre to oversee the process and ensure the cuisine is prepared as intended.
For Indian women’s hockey team striker Lalremsiami, the experience has offered athletes more than just a taste of Japan. “Some of us are used to eating sushi, but for a lot of the athletes it was their first taste of Japanese food. Since we have been experiencing the cuisine for a while now, we know what ingredients go into a particular dish and what to expect on our plate. The containers have given us an experience of what to expect in terms of accommodation,” said the youngster.
The idea, according to Sudhakaran, is simple – make Japan feel a little less foreign before the athletes get there.

briefs.headline: Glad to be back at the GCL, says Carlsen
briefs.bodyText:
Chess is finding newer fans. Five-time World champion Magnus Carlsen feels that has been the case for the last five or six years across the world.
“We are still finding different ways to present chess,” said the Norwegian on the eve of the Global Chess League, which kicks off here on Saturday. “For me it is interesting to be part of these innovative events (such as the GCL and the Total Chess World Championship Tour). There is a lot of enthusiasm to present chess in the best way possible.”
Carlsen is glad to be back at the GCL after a year’s interval. “We had a couple of really frustrating years for the team (Alpine Pipers) when I was playing,” he said. “And then when I was away, the team won the title. So, this time I am just trying to do my best to not do any worse than last year.”
Unlike Carlsen, Viswanathan Anand, also a five-time World champion, is playing for a new team this year – PBG Alaskan Knights. “Every year you have to come with a positive attitude,” he said. “We have a great team...and my role is just that of a player (and not a mentor).”
Javokhir Sindarov, who will be challenging D. Gukesh for the World title later this year, said he wasn’t thinking about that match at the moment. “I have enjoyed playing in every season of the GCL,” he said. “I am excited that I will be playing on the first board this year and I will try my best to help my team (Fyers American Gambits) win the tournament.”
Among the biggest attractions of the league is the Turkish prodigy Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus. He is making his GCL debut and is part of Alaskan Knights. “It is going to be an amazing experience for me to play along with Vishy (Anand) and Arjun (Erigaisi),” he said.
Like him, Divya Deshmukh is also playing at the GCL for the first time. And she is looking forward to the experience of playing without increment though she is also a bit wary of it. “I would love to flag some of my opponents (in the time scramble),” said the Women’s World Cup winner.
The GCL’s chairman Peeyush Dubey said the GCL proved chess could also be a festival. “And we have support from some of the biggest companies in the world,” he said.
